Answer for Department of Railways and Canals.
Pictou, N.S., January 20, 1912. Honourable Frank Cochrane, M.P.,
Minister of Railways and Canals,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Sir,-Referring to the case of Joseph Veniot, which was heard by me to-day in Pictou, I would ask you to kindly instruct me whether you wish to have a verbatim copy of the evidence.
There is another point on which I would like to receive your instructions. When this case was called this morning Mr. John U. Ross, a barrister of this town, asked permission to appear and represent Veniot at the hearing. I told him that while I would not object to his presence or the presence of tiny one interested in the proceedings, I could not allow counsel to be heard either for or against any of the parties interested in this case, herein following the rule that was laid down by Mr. J. T. Ross, commissioner appointed for similar work in 1896-97.
At the conclusion of the evidence of each witness I asked Veniot whether he wished to have witnesses asked any questions and put to them all the questions that he suggested. Even though counsel was excluded I found that this case took several hours to hear.
Kindly instruct me as to what procedure you wish followed in regard to this point. I am inclined to think that if counsel is admitted at these investigations, they will be interminably prolonged and it will be slow work with the long list of cases that are liable to arise requiring investigation.
I would also suggest that the department might cause a pass for use on the Intercolonial railway to be issued to me as commissioner, in order to avoid the very large amount of additional accounting that will be necessary in connection with the daily disbursements for tickets. As it is necessary to go to practically every part of the eight counties included in the jurisdiction assigned to me, there will be a great deal of travel to and fro and some ground will have to be covered and recovered possibly twro or three times within the same week.
It appears to me, therefore, that it would save a great deal of additional and unnecessary work if a pass covering a limited time wrere to issue in this connection.
I have the honour to be, Sir,	.
Your obedienc servant,
(Sgd) Henry P. Duchemin,
Commissioner.
Ottawa, 24th January, 1912.
Dear Sir,-I have yours of January 20, in reference to the procedure to be followed in the investigations held by you. It is not necessary to go to the expense of having a verbatim copy of the evidence taken and I feel that you have taken the right course in the matter of counsel, as to permit counsel to be heard and to cross-

examine would interminably prolong these matters, as you state, and there is the added fact that the precedent quoted by you could scarcely be objected to.
The transportation asked for by you will be forwarded to-day.
Yours very truly,
Henry P. Duchemin,
Barrister, etc., Sydney, C.B.

subtopic: JURISDICTION OF THE ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE MAGISTRATES.
speechtext: I call the attention of the Minister of Justice to a dispatch from Dawson which appeared in the press two days ago, to the effect that a conviction for larceny by one of the Mounted Police magistrates had been quashed because, in the opinion of the judge, the Mounted Police had no jurisdiction. Has my hon. friend received any information upon the subject, or has he communicated with Dawson about the matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: JURISDICTION OF THE ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE MAGISTRATES.
speechtext:
The matter has not
come to my attention. I will ascertain what the situation is.

I wish to rise to a question of privilege. It is a question which affects the dignity of the House and the veracity of a minister of the Crown. I regret that I am forced to raise this question in the absence of the hon. Minister of Militiar, as it particularly affects him, but the matter is of such moment that I have no doubt the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who is now leading the House, will bring it to the attention of the minister concerned. On Monday, the 23rd of February, the Minister of Militia made this statement (Hansard, p. 1074):
The story goes that a certain distinguished gentleman, the ex-Minister of Agriculture and some of his friends in this House had mortgages on a lot of swamp property around Farnham. It was supposed to be used for the raising of tobacco, but it had ceased to be used in that way. Consequently, these gentlemen could not get the amount of their mortgages out of the place. One gentleman said: [DOT] Let us lay out a military camp there.' Reports were immediately forthcoming from two distinguished officers of the service that this was a magnificent site for a camp, and accordingly Farnham camp was unloaded on the Militia Department for a fabulous sum.
These gentlemen received a rake-off for the mortgages which they could not collect in any other way. I understand that both of them had held seats on the Liberal side of the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I beg to say to the hon. member that in my judgment he is out of order. It is not, as I understand it, a question of privilege affecting the hon. member or perhaps any other member of this House. The party against whom the statement was made is not a member of this House, and therefore the statement could not affect any member of the House; so that I think it can hardly be regarded as a question of privilege.

If you rule, Mr'. Speaker, that I am out of order I will go on with the question later in the day. But I submit that this is a question that affects not' the dignity of any particular member in the House, but the dignity of the House through the fact that a minister of the Crown

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It does not affect the
privilege of any member of the House.

What I was going to say, if you had allowed me to finish my sentence, was that the charge is that the Minister of Militia has supplied false information to members of this House, and as a member of this House I was rising in my place to complain of the false information that was supplied to us. If 1 am out of order-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member is out of order and it will be apparent to him that he is violating two rules: first, it is not a matter of privilege in the House; and, secondly, if the allegation is with respect to some person outside of this House it would be a violation of the rule which prevents any member of the House bringing in newspapers or other outside information to contradict the statement of a member of this House.

My hon. friend was just stating a case, but he did not finish his statement of that case. He was referring to the fact that a member of this House, within the knowledge of everybody, had made a certain statement. I do not know what my hon. friend was going on to say, but I think in all fairness to him we should know exactly -what he is going to say before we say it is out of order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman was reading from ' Hansard ' a statement with reference to a certain occurrence which took place in this House the other day, and which referred to the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Hughes). The statement he was reading referred to an outsider, not to a member of this House, and if the allegation was incorrect that fact could only be proven by an outsider. Therefore, it would be bringing information from an outsider to contradict a statement made by a member of this House, which is not permissible.

I had not spoken of an outsider at all; I had simply risen to state my case. It will be readily understood that before a verdict can be rendered in a case the facts must be stated, but if Your Honour \vill not allow me to make a statement of the facts I will resume my seat.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Sitting in the Chair, I knew what the facts related to. The hon. gentleman was reading the statement out of ' Hansard '; therefore, I was quite aware what it related to. I spoke so as to prevent going on with a discussion which seemed to me to be useless.

If Your Honour knew what he was speaking of, Your Honour could not know what he was going to conclude with. My hon. friend had a right to. state the point-it may be out of order or it may be in order, but it seems to me that it is impossible to say whether my hon. friend is in order or not until ho has stated what the point is.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman stated that an allegation which had been made as to an outsider was absolutely untrue; therefore, he was making a statement which could only be supported by evidence coming from outside, which evidence is not admissible in this House.
I understand that my hon. friend was reading what had been reported in ' Hansard,' and that he was proceeding to his conclusion but that he was interrupted before he had come to the conclusion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: But the hon. member afterwards stated what he was referring to and he said that the statement was absolutely untrue. It was this statement which was referred to, and he was endeavouring to contradict it by means which were out of order.

Might I suggest that the question is not that of the Farnham camp, but the question is that of the veracity of a minister, and surely there must be some means by which the House can protect itself against statements made on behalf of the Government, which lack veracity.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The ruling of the Chair must stand until it is appealed against.
What is the ruling of the Chair, may I ask ? Is it that my hon. friend (Mr. Devlin) cannot proceed to make his statement ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes.
Then, I appeal from your ruling.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Devlin, member for Wright, rises to a question of privilege, namely, that a certain statement made by an hon. member of this House was untrue, the statement applying to a certain person not a member of this House; Mr. Speaker ruled that this was not a question of privilege. Sir Wilfrid Laurier appealed from the ruling of the Chair.
The question is: shall the ruling of the Chair be sustained ?

That is not a statement of the case. The statement of the case is this: My hon. friend from Wright was proceeding to state what he called a question of privilege, and he was interrupted by Mr. Speaker on the ground that the question was not one of privilege. I interposed and said that he should be allowed to make his case. I put the question: If he could not be allowed to make his case, and you, Sir, said ' No.' Therefore I appealed from your ruling. My point is that my hon. friend from Wright was not allowed to make his case, and that is the point upon which I appeal from your ruling.
I did not say that the Minister's statement was untrue, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The second time the hon. member for Wright got up he stated that the allegation was made not against a member of this House, but a person outside of the House, and that it was untrue. I ruled that, as it did not refer to a member of this House, his statement was not admissible here and that it was not a question affecting the privilege of any

member of this House. For both of these reasons I thought his statement was out of order.

That is only part of the case. I put the question direct: Will you allow my hon. friend from Wright (Mr. Devlin) to state his case? and you ruled that you would not allow him. That was the point upon which I appealed from your ruling.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
As I understood the
matter, the second time that the hon. member for Wright spoke he finished stating his case.
No.
I had just begun.
Just begun.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It seems to me that it
is a question that ought to be resolved in a very simple way. His Honour the Speaker has ruled-and without looking at the authorities I think he has ruled correctly-that a matter raised in respect to some person not in the House is not a question of privilege in the way in which this has been brought forward. If the hon. gentleman from Wright has a question of privilege which comes -within the decision of the Speaker, there ought to be no objection to his stating it; but if he is proceeding to state a case which is contrary to the decision which has already been rendered by Mr. Speaker and which commends itself to my judgment, then I think he has already stated his case sufficiently to enable Mr. Speaker to arrive at the decision he did.

My right hon. friend is altogether in error. My hon. friend from Wright was proceeding to state a case. I did not know what the matter was; I did not know to what point he was coming. Before proceeding to tender his statement, he was simply reciting a case, _ upon which probably he wanted to make a motion or to which he wanted to call the attention of the House, when he was interrupted by Mr. Speaker. There was some further discussion. Then I put the question to Mr. Speaker: Will you not allow my hon. friend to state his case? Mr. Speaker stated:	No, I will not allow
him. It is upon that point that I appeal from your ruling, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. member for-
Wright had stated his case sufficiently to
enable His Honour the Speaker to judge that it was in respect of a person not a member of this House. I for one cannot see the advantage of making any further statement unless the hon. member for Wright is in a position to affirm that his further observations will bring the case within the ruling laid down by Mr. Speaker.

With your permission,
Mr. Speaker, and for the information of the right hon. the Prime Minister, I might state that I rose to a question of privilege, as I believed that the substance of what I was going to submit to the Chair and to this House was sufficient to show that the dignity of this House had been affected inasmuch as the veracity of a minister of the Crown had been called in question, and that it was supposed that the minister of the Crown had furnished this House with false information. I was proceeding to state upon what I based my allegation and to give to the Chair the facts of the case when. Mr. Speaker simply said that I could not state my case to the House. Thereupon the right hon. the leader of the Opposition appealed from the ruling of Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would think that if the varacity of any hon. member is called in question by some one outside of the House, that is a question of privilege for the hon. member whose varacity is called in question and not for any other member of the House, so far as the question of privilege is concerned.

My point js
simply this, whether or not we shall have the right of freedom of speech. My hon. friend (Mr. Devlin) may be right or he may be wrong. No one can say whether he is right or wrong until he has stated his case, and he has not been allowed to do so.
Mr. M^IGHEN: The right hon. gentleman must admit that the hon. member for Wright went so far as to say that the case consisted in the submitting of an allegation made by the hon. Minister of Militia, as reported in 'Hansard'. He proceeded to say that this allegation was false. He then read from the allegation sufficiently far to bring to the notice of Mr. Speaker the statement made by the hon. Minister of Militia. That being the case, it became clear at once that it could not be a question

of privilege on the part of any hon. member of this House, because it did not affect the honour or privilege of any member of this House. At that point the Speaker ruled that the hon. member for Wright was out of order. If Mr. Speaker, before' he renders a decision, has to wait until an hon. member has stated his whole case, what is the value of ruling out something that is already in?

Mr. Speaker came to a conclusion before my hon. friend from Wright had made his statement. That is what I object to. I asked Mr. Speaker to allow my hon. friend to finish his statement, but he would not allow him to do that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot see that my right hon. friend is quite logical in that. If the hon. member for Wright is admittedly proceeding to make a statement which contravenes a rule that the Speaker has already laid down, there is no interference with freedom of speech in that regard, because according to the premises it is a statement which he ought not to make, and which is not a matter of privilege according to the principle already laid down by the Speaker. If the hon. member for Wright is willing to declare that the statement he proposes to make is within the rule laid down by the Speaker, there ought to be no objection to iris proceeding with that statement. But, I inferred, I think rightly, that the statement has proceeded sufficiently far to enable the Speaker to see that it was not a matter of privilege. Therefore it seems to me that the Speaker properly intervened.
I appeal to my right hon. friend; the Minister of Militia made a statement with respect to a certain member.	.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.	.

With respect to one who is not in the House. There are many things that can be done upan such a statement. He might have desired to call the attention of the Minister of Militia to that statement and to ask him, if it was incorrect, to retract it. That is perfectly in order. The Minister of Militia made a grave allegation against an hon. gentleman, and although he is not a member of the House, I believe he has a right to his fair name. If it is shown to the hon. Minister of Militia that he made a false statement, it 
is within the rules of the House to bring it to his attention and to ask him to correct it. My hon. friend from Wright, however, was not allowed to proceed at all. That is the only point with which I find fault, namely if Mr. Speaker has ruled: No, I will not hear any more; I decide at once. That is the matter upon which I appealed to the judgment of the House, viz, that my hon. friend be allowed to make his statement.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the right hon. the leader of the Opposition scarcely does me justice in that statement, because the hon. member for Wright was twice upon his feet. The first time, he referred to a statement made by'the hon. Minister of Militia and commenced to read the ' Hansard ' report of that statement. I sent for the Clerk of the House to consult him as to whether that was in order or not and he agreed with me that it was not in order. The second time the hon. member was on his feet, he stated that the i3tatement was made against an hon. gentleman who is not in the House and that the statement was absolutely false. I ruled that, in the first place, it was not a question of privilege, because it did not affect the privilege of any member sitting in the House, and in the second place, if his allegation was correct, it must be substantiated by evidence brought from outside this House, to contradict the statement of a member in this House. That is not permissible. I wish to say one thing more with regard to what I conceive to be my duty. The rule as laid down, both in the British House and in this House, is as plain, I think, as the English language can make it and it is that, while others may raise a point of order or objection, it is the duty of the Speaker, when anything is said that is out of order, to immediately call attention to it; which I did, of course,'knowing what was referred to, and-

But, Mr. Speaker, if you had allowed my hon. friend from Wright to proceed with his case, he would have read these words:
The story goes that a certain distinguished gentleman, the ex-Minister of Agriculture and some of his friends in this House had mortgages on a lot of swamp property around Farnham.
So, the statement affected not only the ex-Minister of Agriculture but certain members of this House. But you did not

allow my hon. friend to go on with his speech. Had he been permitted to go on, he would have shown that you were in the wrong. I put the question: Do I understand that you will not allow my hon. friend to proceed with his case? And you said: No. And thereupon I appealed from your ruling.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would like the right hon. member to make his statement setting forth what he holds to have been improper in the ruling, and submit it to the House.

I will make it in this way: The hon. member for Wright was proceeding to challenge some statements made by the hon. Minister of Militia against the ex-Minister of Agriculture and certain members of this House. He was interrupted by Mr. Speaker, who told him that the matter was not one of privilege. Thereupon, the member for Quebec East (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) put the question whether or not Mr. Speaker would allow the hon. member for Wright to proceed with his case. Mr. Speaker ruled that he would not allow the hon. member to proceed. Thereupon there was an appeal from the ruling of the Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman is not exactly correct 4 p.m. in this respect, that he was three times on his feet, and it was only at the third time that the ruling was challenged.

I was three times on my feet to urge that my hon. friend might be allowed to proceed. When, at last, I put the question direct whether he might proceed or not, and you decided against him, I appealed from your ruling.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have only to say, with reference to the ruling on the reading of ' Hansard ' to which the right hon. member has referred, that the emphatic statement was made by the hon. member for Wright that it did not apply to members of this House, but that it referred to a gentleman not now a member of the House. If the hon. member for Wright had been prepared to say that the statement referred to members of this House-whether friends of the gentleman named or otherwise, would have made no difference-I would have taken his word. That statement was not made, but the emphatic statement was made that it did not refer to any gentleman who is now a member of this House.

I did not consider that the time had come when I should have said to whom it referred. I was quoting language officially reported in this House:
The story goes that a certain distinguished gentleman, the ex-Minister of Agrieulture, and some of his friends in this House had mortgages on a lot of swamp property around Farnham.
In this I was quoting language which had been used in this House on the 23rd of February by the hon. Minister of Militia. And when I said that this affected the dignity of this House, I think I was within my rights. But you would not allow me to proceed with the statement of my case, though you could not know what case I was going to state.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. member for Wright if he is prepared to say that this has reference to members of this House. If he does, he would be in order; if not, he would be out of order, in my judgment.

I ask the right to proceed with the case I was going to state to the House, but I am prepared to submit to your ruling. I cannot give you the conclusion of the case before I have stated the facts, and if you declare I cannot proceed with my case, as I say, I submit to your ruling.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The rule is that a member must state his question of privilege, and it does not necessarily follow, in my judgment, that he can go on and make a long argument or read documents on the subject before the Speaker is given means of judging whether it is a matter of privilege or not.
My objection is that you could not form your judgment as to that question until the hon. gentleman had come to a conclusion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member should state his question of privilege.

I think I had reached the word ' Farnham', but perhaps I had better begin again:
The story goes that a certain distinguished gentleman, the ex-Minister of Agriculture, and some of his friends in this House had mortgages on a lot of swamp property around Farnham, It was supposed to be used for the raising of tobacco, but it had ceased to be used in that way. Consequently, these gentlemen could not get the amount of their mortgages out of the place. One gentleman said: 'Let us lay

out a military camp there.' Reports were immediately forthcoming- from two distinguished officers of the service that this was a magnificent site for a camp, and accordingly Farnham camp was unloaded on the Militia Department for a fabulous sum. These gentlemen received a rake-off for the mortgages which they could not collect in any other way.
It was the ex-Minister of Agriculture and some of his friends who are mernbers of this House who, according to this statement, had received this rake-off. {Reading):
I understand that both of them had held seats on the Liberal side of the House. My hon. friend cannot find an officer in the eastern townships, be he a Liberal or be he a Conservative, who will say that one can ride for a distance of a hundred yards in a straight line in Farnham camp without getting into a bog hole and losing the shoes off his horse's feet. One of those officers who made the report was one day talking to a colonel and he said, 'Don't you think it will make a magnificent site?' The colonel replied, 'There is just one thing it lacks.' 'What is that?' said the officer. ' Why,' he says, 4 It requires to be planked over.'
An hon. Member:	Was _it Mr. Sydney
Fisher?
Mr. Hughes: Mr. Sydney Fisher, ex-Minister of Agriculture; certainly.
When the Minister of Militia, whom I am glad to see in his seat now, made this statement, he referred to the ex-Minister of Agriculture and to certain members of this House as having received a rake-off. We have a statement, published in a newspaper this morning, purporting, to be made by Mr. Sydney Fisher. It says-
Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is distinctly out of order, because it is not permissible to bring into the House any paper or document printed outside, for the purpose of contradicting statements made by a member of the House.

I will not use the newspaper. It is publicly reported that Mr. Sydney Fisher, one of the gentlemen named, has said that the Minister of Militia was conveying to this House false information, in which there was not a word of truth.
I submit that the hon. gentleman is out of order.
Sit down.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member rises to a point of order.

The hon. gentleman,
in what lie has said, has made it plain

that he is speaking here on behalf of Mr. Sydney Fisher, and his alleged question of privilege has to do with importing here a defence on behalf of Mr. Sydney Fisher, who is not a member of this House. Prime Minister, and to ask him, as the Minister of Militia was not in his seat, to convey to the hon. speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: So far as I am concerned, it does not seem to me that the hon. member for Wright (Mr. Devlin) has raised a question of privilege at all.

Do we understand from my right hon. friend that the Minister of Militia may throw taunts against a member of this House, and that the matter being brought up "by an hon. gentleman on this side, it does not constitute a question of privilege? The Minister of Militia said the other day:
The story goes that a certain distinguished gentleman, the ex-Minister of Agriculture, and some of his friends in this House had mortgages on a lot of swamp property around Farnham.

Mr. SAM. HUGHES: No.

Will the
minister, outside this House, and under his own signature, repeat what he has said?
I am delighted to see the leader of the Opposition getting a little vitality.
Order.
You are a dead man yourself.

Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance) moved second reading of Bill No. 70, respecting Trust Companies.
He said:	This is a measure to provide
general legislation for the incorporation and regulation of trust companies. In this matter the Dominion has not, as the House is aware, exclusive jurisdiction, as it has in the case of banks. Most of the trust companies carrying on business in the Dominion of Canada are incorporated under provincial authority. Many companies have, however, come to Parliament for incorporation, and hitherto incorporation has been granted in two ways, 72
either by letters patent under the Companies Act of the Dominion or by Special Act of this Parliament. Under the Companies Act, the Secretary of State has power to issue charters incorporating companies for any of the purposes or objects to which the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada extends, except the construction and working of railways or telegraph or telephone lines, the business of insurance, the business of a loan company, the business of banking and the issue of paper money. Trust companies are therefore not within the exception, and in consequence have been incorporated in the past by letters patent issued by the Secretary of State.	Under the
authority of the Companies Act, letters patent have been granted over a period of years conferring exceedingly wide powers on trust companies. For the information of the House, and in order to show why I desire to enact that hereafter no trust company shall be incorporated by letters patent, I shall refer to some of the powers which have been conferred upon trust companies by the issue of letters patent. Into the question as to whether the Secretary of State has any discretion as to the powers which he will grant by the issue of letters patent, it is not necessary to enter now. I have before me a copy of the charter of a trust company incorporated about a year ago, and by it the following, among many other powers, have been granted:
To accept, fulfil and execute any trust committed to the company by any person, corporation or court of justice on such terms as may be agreed upon or as the court shall approve of, and take, receive, hold, convey and lease all assets and property, both real and personal, which may be granted, deposited, committed or conveyed to the company with its assent upon such trust or trusts, and to manage estates of deceased or insolvent persons and to act as executor, administrator, trustee, receiver, sequestrator, assignee, curator to insolvent's estates, guardian, committee of the person, tutor or minors or curator to interdicted persons.
Then these further powers are granted, to which I wish to draw the attention of the House:
To promote, organize and manage financial, commercial, industrial, trading, development, mercantile and other companies and corporations ; to subscribe for, purchase, acquire, underwrite, hold and sell or otherwise dispose of, on commission or otherwise and to deal in the shares, bonds or other securities of any company or corporation notwithstanding the provisions of section 44 of the said Act.

Further:
To acquire by purchase, lease, exchange or other legal title and to sell and otherwise deal in the business, property, francmses, rights and undertaking of any financial, commercial, manufacturing, industrial, development or other trading corporation of any kind or of any firm, partnership or individual for the purpose of promoting, enlarging and organizing companies, and to carry on the same and to manage, operate and carry on any business, property and undertakings so acquired and to assume the liabilities thereof.
Further:
To enter into any arrangement for the sharing of profits or union of interest, joint adventure, reciprocal concession or otherwise, with any person or company carrying on or about to carry on any business similar to that of the company hereby incorporated and to promote or assist in promoting and to become a shareholder in any such company.
To advance money or guarantee the obligations or contracts of or otherwise assist or aid in any manner any company whose shares of capital stock, bonds or other obligations are held by the company.
To issue fully paid-up and non-assessable shares, bonds, and other securities of the company in payment in whole or in part for any real or personal property, rights, franchises or other assets acquired by the company by any title or for services rendered by way of promotion or otherwise.
To invest arid deal with the moneys of the company not immediately required in such securities and in such manner as may be from time to time determined.
I am sure I voice the view of every hon. gentleman in this House, that powers so wide, so varied and so unrelated should not be granted to companies which enter into such intimate and fiduciary relationship with the public as trust companies do. I think it must be clear that the Companies Act, under authority of which letters patent have been issued in the past ten years conferring powers as wide as those I have mentioned upon trust companies, must be defective.

Is it the intention to
amend the Companies Act also?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is my intention to provide that hereafter no trust company, as defined in this Act, shall be incorporated by letters patent. I find that 31 trust companies have been incorporated by letters patent since 1901. Of those, 20 have been incorporated during the past two years. It would appear [DOT] therefore that the number has increased in recent years, and it is quite evident that incorporators are desirous of obtaining the very wide powers which they are able to obtain under the Companies Act rather than come to Par-

liament for special legislation giving them the power of carrying on the business of trust companies throughout the Dominion.
Will this legislation affect the charters or powers of existing companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
1 am in favour of the minister bringing in a Bill such as he describes. For the past few years, in the Banking and Commerce Committee, when the various trust corporations come up for charters, we had sometimes great difficulty in reconciling them to an even basis, as it were. We had constant

applications to widen their powers, and I think it was the Banking and Commerce Committee really that urged the minister last year and the year before to draft such a Bill as he is proposing now. I cannot say anything against it, and I have no doubt the Banking and Commerce Committee will give it very serious consideration and do all the amending of it that is necessary.

Mr. Speaker, might I first congratulate my hon. friend (Mr. White) on his return to his duties in the House after his illness. Speaking merely from memory, it seems to me that the adoption by Parliament of this Bill would necessitate an amendment to the Companies Act and also a change in the form used by the State Department under which letters patent are issued. These are mere matters of detail, but I draw attention to them now, so that they may be dealt with concurrently with the consideration of this measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend's suggestion occurred to me and it has been considered. The opinion is that, having regard to the fact that this Trust 'Company Act is a general Act and that it especially provides no trust company shall, after the passing of this Act, be incorporated by letters patent under tne provisions of part 1 of the Companies Act, chapter 79 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, no substantial amendment of the Companies Act will be necessary, because any lawyer, knowing as he should know that there is general legislation affecting trust companies, would have before him this provision in this Act respecting trust companies and therefore would not apply for letters patent under the Companies Act because the right of obtaining such letters patent has been done away with. Nevertheless, for greater clearness and certainly I would see no objection to putting trust companies in the exceptions in the Companies Act and then the public would not be in any way misled as to the rights of obtaining charters by letters patent.
That would prevent a possible slip which might occur in the department when the Secretary of State or the Under Secretary was not present.

The Act seems certainly well conceived and there can be very little doubt that such legislation is becoming more and more a necessity. The

fact, which is now patent to everybody, that trust companies are very largely resorted to for the administration of the estates of widows and orphans makes it all the more necessary that adequate safeguards should be taken to make sure that the money put in their hands is absolutely beyond the possibility of any misfortune. My hon. friend has made a statement which goes to show the necessity of having such legislation at a very early date. He said that during the last two years some 20 trust companies had been incorporated. That number is certainly startling, and there is reason to doubt that they are all of such a character as could be desired. Has my hon. friend any information as to whether these companies which have received their incorporation are now in operation ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am unable to say whether they have been organized. The charters have certainly been granted, and I should presume most of them would be alive, so to speak, at the present time.

They have legal life, but whether they are actually living is another matter. My hon. friend, in answer to a question put to him, stated that he had not fully made up his mind whether or not this Act should be made retroactive, as he saw very considerable difficulty in that. I quite agree with him. The reasons may be strong and many why it should be retroactive, but it is only in very extreme cases now that Parliament will agree to make any law retroactive. I suggest to my hon. friend that all of these companies which have been granted charters but are not yet in operation, might be very properly brought within the terms of this Act. If a company is in operation it is a vested interest which Parliament would hesitate to interfere with, but in case of a company having a charter and not being in full operation, the Act might very well apply to it.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.

Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 83, respecting loan companies.
He said:	After the general explanation
which I have given as to the object of the legislation which I.am introducing to regulate trust companies, it will not be necessary for -me to say much with respect to this Bill which has the same purpose in
i EBRUARY 26, 1914
view, namely, to create a general act under which loan companies may be incorporated.
I may say, briefly, that loan companies invest their own funds, funds which they have received by way of deposit and moneys which they have received from the sale of their debentures. In the past, loan companies have been incorporated under Dominion authority by letters pat. ent, and by special acts as in the case of trust companies. The powers which I confer upon loan companies under the provisions of this Bill, are those which have been approved by the Banking and Commerce Committee and by Parliament as proper and necessary for the conduct of the business of loan companies throughout the Dominion. I have imposed certain restrictions with respect to the holdings of real estate, and I have provided new legislation requiring returns and financial statements to be sent to the minister or Department of Finance giving full information as to the financial condition of loan companies having Dominion charters, and details of their investments. This will, I think, be very much in the public interest, because after all the best safeguard which the public can have against the operation of companies, which might be of an improper character, is publicity. Provision is also being made for inspection by the treasury board in the event of a report being made by the minister calling attention to irregularities or features in the returns which he thinks may require attention. Loan companies have been incorporated under the Companies' Act to the number of 13 only, whereas by Act of Parliament 38 have been incorporated during the same period, since 1872. That shows clearly that part 3 of the Companies' Act, which provides for the incorporation of loan companies, has been regarded as inadequate by persons seeking the incorporation of loan companies. Whether it is that the powers are not sufficiently definite, or that other provisions of the Companies' Act are defective in so far as loan companies are concerned, I am not in a position to say. I will now move the second reading of this Bill, on the understanding that it be referred to the Select Standing Committee on Banking and Commerce.
Mr. MeKENZIE:	Might I ask whether
any effort has been made to secure uniformity in these laws. We have nine legislatures in the Dominion, all of which can legislate on the same subject, and it i3 highly desirable there should be some uniformity. One company getting
its powers from the local legislature may be side by side with a company receiving its charter from this House. It will be apparent to the minister that it is highly desirable that the powers of these companies should be of the same extent, and that the laws should be, as far as possible, uniform. I would suppose that the Department of Finance and the Department of Justice would possibly meet with very little objection from the provincial jurisdiction in bringing about uniformity in the law. I would suggest to the minister, in passing, that there is here an opportunity for the Department of Finance and the Department of Justice to try and obtain uniformity in regard to trust companies and loan companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I appreciate the importance of the matter to which my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) has drawn my attention, and to which I have given some consideration. I have held the view that, while unquestionably the Dominion has jurisdiction to incorporate trust companies, this is a class of company that might well be incorporated by the provinces. There may be a difference of opinion as to that, but certainly most trust companies carrying on business throughout the Dominion are operating under provincial and not Dominion charter. On the other hand, the business of a loan company, I think, properly comes under the jurisdiction of the Dominion because in one feature of its business it is analogous to banking, namely, taking deposits from the public. I did consider, before introducing these Bills, whether it might not be proper for me to take up with the several provinces, if I might without offence, the question of obtaining uniform legislation in reference to this very important subject. Whether that is feasible or not, I do not know. I have already received a request from the authorities of two of the provinces to send them a copy of this legislation and what I think they have in view is precisely what my hon. friend has brought to the attention of the House. Whether the several provinces would be willing, because there is no question as to their jurisdiction, to adopt legislation of this character, I am unable to say, but I shall undertake to forward to each of the attorneys general, or the provincial secretaries, a copy of this law when it is enacted. In that way it will be before them and they can take such action as they deem proper. If there is anything I can do to promote uniformity I shall be only too glad to do

it, because I have the same view upon that point as has my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), namely, that the most important business conducted by trust companies is as executors, administrators, curators or guardians of deceased persons and consequently trustees for widows and orphans. Therefore, I think their operations should be surrounded with all possible safeguards in the public interest consistent with their being enabled to carry on their business with reasonable freedom.

It would be desirable if there could be uniformity between provincial and Dominion legislation, but I am sorry to say that I do not see much hope of that. Can my hon. friend tell me the position of the dispute between the Dominion and the provinces in regard to the power claimed by the provinces to create companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the absence of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), I am not in a position to make a statement as to that. I could only give my understanding of it, but that might be incorrect. I am quite aware of the significance of the remarks made by my right hon. friend and of their bearing upon the respective jurisdictions of the provinces and of the Dominion, and of the right of the province to exclude or to authorize companies having Dominion powers to do business within the provinces. Not having definite information, I refrain from making any statement on the point.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I should like to say
for the information of the House, because it is desirable that we should follow the rules of procedure, that while on the second reading of a Bill a minister has the right to speak twice, it is not permissible to speak back and forth across the floor of the House before the House has gone into Committee of the Whole, as some hon. members have done. I should have intimated to the House, before the minister spoke a second time, that it was open to any hon. member to make any observation that he desired to make, but I did not do so.

My hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. White) and my hon. friend the member for Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) have been discussing the importance of uniformity in legislation and more particularly the special phase of uniformity which formed the subject of
[Mr. W. T. White. 1
their remarks. May I suggest that to secure further imiformity my hon. friend the Minister of Finance should repeal part 3 of the Companies Act? Part 3 forms a very considerable portion of the Companies Act, extending from sections 177 to 275 inclusive. 1 think that as a necessary sequence of the legislation introduced by my hon. friend, with which, from my experience in the State Department I am in hearty accord, an Act should be introduced repealing that portion of the Companies Act.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.

The House in Committee of Supply. Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
Arts and Agriculture-division of entomology,

I understand this is an
entirely new item. Would the minister be good enough to explain it?

This is new this year,
simply because in past years we did this work under the next item, which is for the administration and enforcement of the Destructive Insects and Pest Acts. A great deal of the work of the Entomological Branch has nothing to do with the experimental farm, and for convenience of working we have decided to make it a separate branch. This is why this new vote appears for the first time. ,We have officers at work in different parts of the country and a great deal of expense is entailed upon us by the campaign we are carrying on against the brown-tail moth and the gypsy moth in the Maritime provinces. These pests constitute one of the greatest dangers we have in this country.

The creation of this branch will not be criticised by anybody because we appreciate the importance of such a branch. Would my hon. friend give some information as to the organization of the branch, its personnel, and the work it is doing.

The branch will be presided over by Dr. Hewitt, who has been at the head of the division of entomologists. He will have one or two of the other officials formerly connected with that work, and probably only the apiarist will be at the Central Farm. These gentlemen will issue the various bulletins, which in them-

selves take almost one-third of this item, in connection with the methods of counteracting the ravages of destructive insects. They will carry on field, laboratory and investigation work. Our idea is to put the whole of this most important work upon a systematic basis and to keep trained scientific entomologists constantly in touch with the progress of the work throughout the country.
I spoke of the very important work we are trying to do in regard to the brown-tail and the gypsy moths, which are now invading the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, and which are capable of enormous ravages. When I inform the House that the United States Federal Government and the Governments of the different eastern States have spent, since these pests got a foothold in Massachusetts, which was only in the year 1897, more than ^8,000,000 trying to fight these insects, and not any too successfully, hon. members will thoroughly understand means to prevent their ravages in Canada justifies large expenditure. The brown-tail moth is now in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick covering quite a large area, and the gypsy moth is within forty or fifty miles of New Brunswick at the present time.
What trees do they attack?

The gypsy moth defoliates deciduous and coniferous trees. The brown-tail moth attacks deciduous trees and not coniferous trees. The danger of the brown-tail moth, which is a common European pest, is that it can spread very much more rapidly on this continent. The female moth is a very strong flier, she lays large numbers of eggs and could cover large sections in this country with very great rapidity. These two insects, like some of the worst insects that have appeared on this continent, have come here from Europe and we have not been able to find among our common predacious insects, any insect foe in the larval or in the perfect insect stage to keep them down. Tne consequence is that these insects spread rapidly. Some of the most valuable work which is being done in the United States is the introduction of parasites, both beetles and flies, and we are introducing them also into New Brunswick and Nova Scotia in the hope that they will multiply and keep these mischievous insects under control.
5 p.m. We are now fighting them, in co-operation with the provincial
Governments of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, who are maintaining the same number of inspectors as we are. In the winter we are discovering and destroying the nests, and we intend to carry on a great deal of experimental work during the summer. Although the work is arduous, and I am afraid that the increase of the insect is quite noticeable, I am sure the House will approve such an expenditure.
What area in Nova Scotia has been discovered to he infested with the browndail moth?

Perhaps it might be useful to give the area affected in the United Stated since 1897, when that insect first appeared there. At the present the area infested with the brown-tail moth is
33,000	square miles in the eastern stateB. In the United States the area infested with the gypsy moth is 16,000 square miles. The brown-tail moth, in New Brunswick, is in the counties of St. John, Queens, Sunbury, Charlotte, York and Carleton, covering an area of approximately 6,000 square mileB.
In Victoria, New Brunswick, this moth has done a great deal of harm during the last year or two along the St. John river.

In Nova Scotia, the brown-tail moth is in the counties of Hants, Kings, Annapolis, Digby, Yarmouth and Shelburne, covering an area of 3,200 square miles. There are about 9,200 square miles in Canada infested with the brown-tail moth, as compared with 33,000 square mileB in the United States. The gypsy moth has not yet come to this country; it is about forty or fifty miles south in the state of Maine. We hope during the winter, by constant inspection, by destruction of the nests with the young larvae in them, and by the introduction of these parasites, to make good headway.
When did this pest first make its appearance in eastern Canada?

It was first discovered in Kings County, Nova Scotia, in 1907. That is the first registered discovery. It was introduced into the province by flights of the female moths carried by strong winds from the neighbouring states, and of course it came on lumber and on ships. The first discovery in new Brunswick was m 1911, when it came in on prevailing winds from the state of Maine. It is also brought in on nursery stock. We are main-

taining a very strict inspection over nursery
[DOT] stock.
How long do these moths take to kill a grown tree-one or two years?

I could not say positively as to that. If the foliage of a tree is absolutely denuded by these insects, it would certainly not take more than another year, if the pest came again, because the tree would be so weakened that it would have very little foliage the next year, and would not be able to breathe at all.

Last year considerable damage was done by caterpillars to the fruit trees and also to the maple trees in Canada. Has the hon. minister given any consideration to a method of preventing the caterpillar plague? I am not sure whether it is under provincial or under federal control.

I do not know to what caterpillar my hon. friend is referring.
These insects do practically all their damage in the caterpillar or larval form.
I think my hon. friend must refer to the ordinary tent caterpillar which does a great deal of harm throughout Canada but whose destruction can be accomplished in various ways. It breeds very fast and covers a large area very often, and then, because it is the victim of a number of native parasites, when these parasites multiply it is kept in check. Then, just as with the locust it does not appear for several years when, the parasites having died dawn, the caterpillar gets another start. It is an example of the continued oscillation in nature with which all are familiar. In orchard work it is not hard to control this insect, because its nest can be seen so easily.

What is the
remedy?

The remedy is to spray with arsenical poisons. The caterpillar takes its food by means of its jaws, and so will take in the poison of the spray. Another way is to destroy the nests which appear on the trees.
That is a very slow process, and some other remedy should be discovered.
Is it not better to take off in March or April the nests which are banded around the limb of the trees? I think that was advised in the bulletin issued by the department.

This item covers the expense of bulletins' dealing with all these things, which bulletins are sent out in very large numbers. As to our relation to the work of the provincial governments in these matters of agriculture you can hardly lay down any hard and fast rule, and there must be some overlapping. We wish to make a specialty in dealing with all these things that may fairly be described as interprovincial, that can spread from province to province, and by means of our educational and bulletin work to reach as many people as possible, working, as far as possible, in conjunction with the provincial governments, all of whom of course are interested in such work.

Last yeajr while Parliament was sitting this city was for a time in a most disgusting condition as the result of the caterpillar plague. This is the seat of the federal Government, here is located the Central Experimental Farm, with I suppose, an entomological service. This city also, like others, has its municipal government, and, like others, is under the jurisdiction of the province. I would like to know whose fault it was that we had such an almost unbearable condition as we had last year. I am not suggesting that it was the fault of the Department of Agriculture or of the Government of the day, but I would like to know whose fault it was. Information as to how this pest could be dealt with must have been available here. If the condition which arose was the fault of the civic authorities, I think it would- be right and proper for the Minister of Agriculture to rise in his place and say so, or, if the provincial government was responsible, that should be made known. Certainly it was a terrible condition, that here, in the capital of the country, we were subjected to a disgusting pest which was also damaging to the permanent beauty of the place, and yet no remedy seemed to be applied.

Of course, we all have
a very clear recollection of the condition to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) refers. I cannot see that the duty or responsibility in the matter was ours. We felt the responsibility of giving the information as to methods of cure, and that we did in the most public way, but the application of the remedy, I should think, would be with the local authorities. I am sure the hon. gentleman will agree with me that it is not for the federal Government to clear the streets and back yards of a pest of this kind,

but there is an individual responsibility resting on the citizen, and a civic and provincial responsibility as well. I think we could hardly undertake to deal with a familiar pest of this kind. The only case that would justify our taking direct action would be the incursion of some pest from abroad whose operations are not understood and which had no natural enemies in the country. In such a case, having the scientific equipment and better men than are employed in most localities, we might take hold of the work that would not otherwise be done. But if in this case we give the necessary information-we do very freely-it is the duty of individuals and the civic authorities to attend to the work.

I understood from the hon. minister that in the case of the pest now coming into the Maritime provinces actual work was done by the department. The minister makes a distinction between .a native pest and an imported pest, and I am sorry to know that in case of a recurrence of the conditions of last year, should we be so unfortunate as to be here late in the season, it will not be possible for the department to take active measures in this city against the pest. I do not know what the remedy is, but, while not wishing to relieve the civic authorities of any responsibility, I would respectfully suggest that, in case of a recurrence of the pest this summer, and should Parliament still be in session, the department should depart from the rule the minister has laid down, and, as a matter of fact, relieve the city from the disgusting appearance it had during so many days last year.

I would not like to go so faT as my hon. friend goes. I do not think it is our duty to attend to an evil which is an ordinary occurrence, and the method of dealing with which is known. I draw this distinction: There have been cases in the United States and elsewhere of a foreign pest coming in, jeopardizing a whole industry, and threatening to cover the country with extraordinary rapidity. In such a case interference was necessary. But take a pest which, in some ways, is equally bad, the -common house-fly, a filthy and abominable pest-it would not be said that it was the duty of the federal Government to attend to the business of making [DOT] everybody take the precautions to stamp out this evil. There may be some special responsibility resting upon the Government
with regard to Ottawa because it is the federal capital. So far as we can logically and properly step in and assist, we are only too glad to do so. But I do hot think we should undertake the work of cleaning up every man's garden or saving eveTy shade-tree in Ottawa.
My county grows the finest apples fn Canada-
Oh, oh.
That is a large claim.

As I hear no dissenting voices, I suppose I may assume that I am stating an accepted fact. But last year this pest of caterpillars destroyed some of the beautiful orchards in my county. I hope the Minister of Agriculture will help the apple-growers of Rouville-and the apple-growers of all Canada, or at least of the province of Quebec-if this evil exists only in Quebec-to overcome that plague, and that some of this money will be spent for that purpose; otherwise we may lose the best apple of Canada, the Fameuse, which is grown in the county of Rouville. Will my hon. friend tell the committee whether any part of the moneys which are handed to the provincial governments is devoted to the purpose of banishing this pest from our orchards? I should like to know also how it is that the moneys allotted to the province of Quebec are put, so to speak, in the hands of a guardian. I understand that in the other provinces the moneys are handed to the Minister of Agriculture, whilst in the province of Quebec an exception has been made. Mr. Chapais, whose knowledge of agricultural conditions I do not question, but who, it seems to me, should not have been put over the Minister of Agriculture in the province of Quebec, was given the control of the expenditure of those moneys; at least the Minister of Agriculture in the province of Quebec is obliged to report to Mr. Chapais, who, in turn, reports to my hon. friend the minister. There is quite a feeling in our province about this matter. The other provinces have no such guardian, and surely my hon. friend did not deem that in the province of Quebec there should be one. I may tell my hon. friend that the Minister of Agriculture of the province of Quebec is a real farmer, a man of great knowledge who has made a success of his farming, and has the confidence of the farming communities in that province. What impelled my hon. friend to follow a different course in
11.34

regard to the province of Quebec than that which he followed in respect to the other provinces?

Although this discussion should, perhaps, take place under the regular item, I have no objection to answering my hon. friend's question. I have a very lively recollection, however, of an unfortunate precedent established by my predecessor when, having made an assertion about a certain apple being the finest in the world, he drew down upon his devoted head and upon the House a deluge of talk about the value of apples from every man from an apple growing county in Canada, so I will not enter into the discussion of that matter.
My friends opposite may attempt to banish the county of Rouville under the next redistribution, but I do not wish the Fameuse apple to disappear.

As to the other questions, I have to come back to my original position. The federal Department of Agriculture desires to give all information which will enable the people to combat the ravages of these common pests. When I was a fruit grower myself I had a great deal of experience with these things; I did not get any financial assistance from the Government, but I got the information that enabled me to understand the history of these pests and to become acquainted with the best ways of combating their operations. I found that by a little energy and attention to details, nearly all of these pests could be kept in fair check. With reference to the other question my hon. friend has raised, it would be quite in order for any province under the Agricultural Instruction Act to receive money for the purpose which we have been discussing so long as it be educational or instructional. I do not think the Act could be fairly interpreted as providing that you could give any province money that would enable it to get people to go and do certain work, because that would not be educational or instructional, but I do think it would be well for the Act to enable the provinces to appoint experienced men to go around, as, indeed, is being done, to teach the people the best remedies to adopt. That, I think, is educational and instructional, and therefore it is quite legitimate. As a matter of fact, a considerable portion of these various grants to the provinces, including Quebec, is devoted to things along that line. In Ontario they have given $80,000 [Mr. Lemieux.j
to district representatives, and a large portion of these moneys would be used in the way my hon. friend mentions. With reference to the other part of my hon. friend's remarks, I think he has, perhaps, rather misunderstood the situation. I do not think the word 'guardian' is the right one, as I understand it. There was a question on the Order Paper about a guardian being imposed on the province of Quebec; and, aside from the word ' guardian ' being not quite the correct one, I do not think the office was * imposed.' As my hon. friend knows, under the Act we have the right and authority to ask for statements, examine accounts or appoint any officer to supervise the work. Dr. James, who as my hon. friend knows, is a very capable man, has been all through the West and is not only thoroughly familiar with conditions in the West and East, but has personally known for many years most of the leading men in the provinces connected with agricultural educational work. Before this Bill became law, and long since, he has discussed verbally and by correspondence nearly all these questions. Unfortunately, good a man as Dr. James is, he has only a limited knowledge of the French language, and it was thought advisable, in the interests of the province of Quebec and of the provincial Government-so far as I know no objection was raised on this point when the matter was first discussed-to take the course we did. Both myself and the hon. member for Argenteuil (Mr. Perley) discussed the agreement with Mr. Caron, and all details were carefully gone over. My instructions to Mr. uhapais were to discuss, at any time he or Mr. Caron wished it, the various lines of work-whether anything should be altered; whether anything done would come within the meaning of the Act; what was in the best interests of the province-and to give him advice or assistance when he wanted it. But in no sense of the word was he to dictate to those in authority, or rigidly to put down a line on which they must stand. It is Mr. Chapais' business to see that the work is done and to see, as far as possible, that it is done along the lines laid down by the Act and by the agreement.
Mr. James does this for the other provinces?

He has been keeping in close touch with that work for the other provinces. It is expected that he will have a full report of all work done in the various

provinces to lay before the House, as we have to do under the Act next session.

The hon. member surely does not wish to imply that Sir Lomer Gouin, the Premier of Quebec, and Mr. Caron, the Minister of Agriculture, have no knowledge of the English language. If he knows these gentlemen, he must know that they speak English as well as he does himself.

I do not think my hon. friend's observation is quite in order, because, after all, it is very much better that one of our officers who is dealing with this work should have a thorough knowledge of the language of the province in which the work is carried on.
Mr. Chapais is acting as paid officer of the Department of Agriculture?

He is acting as a federal officer under section 6, I think, of the Act.
Administration and enforcement of the destructive Insect and Pest Act, $50,000.
What success has Mr. Strickland had with the pest known as the cutworm which has been destroying a large amount of grain in southern Alberta?

I am sorry I cannot
give my hon. friend full details, although I will be glad to send him later the actual ' results of the work. That will of course appear in the annual report. Mr. Strickland has done a lot of good work; he is studying more or less the parasites and Remedies that will be helpful. My recollection is that some new species of the cutworm had appeared in the district to which my hon. friend refers.

Mr. Strickland will
be there again this season?
Yes, I suggested that he get back there at a reasonably early date.

How much of this money is
to be expended in Nova Scotia?
More money has probably been spent in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick than in other parts of the Dominion because in those provinces we have been fighting the brown-tail and gypsy moths.
Who has charge of the eradication of the brown-tail moth in Nova Scotia?
Mr. Saunders, I think.

Is that in connection
with the Experimental Farm?

No, it has nothing to
do with it. Mr. Saunders was appointed before I came into office.

I understand there is
another pest in southern Alberta known as the eelworm. Has the minister any information to give in regard to the success in fighting that pest?

I am sorry I cannot
give my hon. friend that information, although I will be glad to send it to him later. Mr. Strickland has been studying both these pests.

The minister should have some idea of the progress made in fighting such serious pests as the cutworm and the eelworm. Have we made substantial progress in fighting these pests, or is the battle still on without a measure of success?

The battle is still on
but there are encouraging signs. I will be glad to refer to the matter again before we get through the Estimates.
If there is any information I think it should be given at the earliest possible date.
The Agricultural Gazette which was discussed the other night will give information like that from month to month.

As the discussion on this item seems to be pretty well exhausted, I would like to call the minister's attention to the Experimental Farm at Fredericton, N.iB., and perhaps the minister will state to the House the reasons, if any, why the Experimental Farm was located at Fredericton; and in the second place why, after they had decided to locate at Fredericton, they did not get hold of" a piece of land good enough to raise produce. The soil of that farm is only one-third or one-quarter of the quality of what we cons der soil in the province of New Brunswick. It was not because good soil could not be had around the city of Fredericton, because the minister knows very well that very good soil is to be found in the province. The farm is some three or four miles below the city and is entirely away from transportation facilities. Two railroads I think run by it, but there is no ready access to it. A farmer who goes to Fredericton and wants to see the Experimental Farm has to drive out three or four miles. Will the minister explain whether any attempt was

made to analyse the soil or was this farm simply bought because somebody wanted to sell it? In going over the Auditor General's Report I notice that A. D. Thomas, whom I know very well-the Minister of Marine knows him also as a sound Conservative to the core; one who never varies for a moment, a Grand Master of the Orangemen, and all those things that go to make a good Tory-I find that Thomas received $1,000 commission for buying a farm that cost only. $13,000, although that is three or four times what it is worth. It seems to me that some explanation of that commission is due, and I think the minister should give it.

The farm at Fredericton was selected after careful consideration. We were anxious to do for New Brunswick what had been done for every other province. It seemed to me that New Brunswick was entitled to have an Experimental Farm. Nobody knows better than my hon. friend that there is great difficulty in the selection of places for experimental farms. There might be a great many other places in New Brunswick which would be admirably suited for one of our farms, the place where my hon. friend comes from for instance, but as Fredericton is centrally situated and is the capital seat of the province, and is accessible, it was considered that, on the whole Fredericton was about as well adapted as any other place could be. I am not saying Oarleton would not have been a good spot. I do not profess to be such an expert as .some men, although I certainly have had a little to do with farming. It is quite obvious that I could not personally select all the farms, but I happened to be at Fredericton and walked over this particular place before it was bought.
Did it impress the minister very favourably?

I do not like to make any animadversions about the soil of New Brunswick, because it is a beautiful province. The reasons that would induce you to buy an experimental farm are not always those which would lead you to buy a farm to makd the most money out of it. We would serve the province better by taking a farm that was fairly typical of a large number of farms, even if it were not in very good condition, than by selecting the best land that we could find in a district and using that for experimental farm purposes. Some 
one would say: Anybody can farm if you buy the best piece of soil that you can find and spend all sorts of money in its operation. My hon. friend says that this farm is four miles from Fredericton. My recollection is that it is not over two miles from Fredericton.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Two or three miles.

It did not strike me that it was more than that; however, that is not a point of very material importance. We sent our own men down to investigate. Mr. Grisdale was down and made a thorough examination of the property from every viewpoint. It was upon his advice and report largely that we came to make up our minds about purchasing this property. I do not think that the price was at all out of the way. In regard to what my hon. friend said about Mr. Thomas, I am afraid I cannot tax my memory with the whole matter, but my recollection of it is that Mr. Thomas had done exceedingly valuable work in connection with the securing of options, that it might otherwise have been difficult to have got on some of these properties. Some of these properties were in a very involved condition, and my recollection is that it was the view of the department that if Mr. Thomas had received $1,000 for securing these options he was instrumental in saving us several times over that amount. I looked into the matter carefully, consulted the deputy minister about it and we felt that we were fully justified in doing what we did and which has been done again and again in the history of the acquisition of experimental farms.

I am sorry not to have heard some justification by the minister for this enormous amount paid to Mr Thomas. I am not here to quarrel with the minister nor with Mr. Thomas. There is no doubt that Mr. Thomas has been a good party worker. He rounded up that particular section of the Orange vote for the Government; it was necessary that he should do it and he will do it again. But it does seem pretty tough that the people of this country have to pay a party heeler a thousand dollars for buying a $10,000 or $12,000 farm. The minister knows that is not right. I realize that he is not responsible; he is only technically responsible.
I do not believe that the minister, left to himself, would pay this man a thousand dollars; he knows better. But political exigencies in New Brunswick are such that the minister has to give way. That is

where I blame the minister. The minister not only had a report from Mr. Grisdale condemning the site in question, but reports on other farms that were so far ahead of this farm that they are not to be mentioned in the same connection. I think he will find a report that Mr. Grisdale wanted to pay $20,000 for another farm that was a farm; that was not only typical of the best land but typical of the poorer land. But unfortunately this farm was in the town of Woodstock and was owned by a bad Grit, and that settled it
Had Mr. Grisdale seen it?

Mr. Grisdale was there
and saw it and if I am not mistaken Mr. Grisdale recommended it. This is a farm of 400 or 500 acres. The owner has lately sold 10 or 15 acres to the Agricultural Society at about $200 an acre.

What is the name of
this farm?

The Smith farm. I am mistaken in saying that he sold it for $200 an acre; he sold it for about $100, or $115 or $120 an acre. There are 200 acres of beautiful upland and 200 acres of rougher land. It would have been typical of practically every quality of soil that is found in New Brunswick. The minister would have had there a real experimental farm on which it would have been possible for him to have demonstrated something. But instead of that he went the way that his political friends told him to go and he bought a farm that is practically nothing more than a sand heap. The minister would not say he would have bought that farm if he had been left to himself? No, the minister would not take that farm as a gift and live on it. There is not a man in this House who would take that farm as a gift and live on it. There is not a plan in this House who would pay $1,090 for the whole of it and yet he pays Duncan Thomas $1,000 for buying it. My hon. friend talks about there being so many options. There are only four of them altogether. He could have got another farm within a mile of Fredericton which is on what is called the Maryland road. I have forgotten the names of those who own it. It is a farm composed of splendid land, a farm which would have been of some value a3 an experimental farm and a farm close to the University of New Brunswick. But, unfortunately, the acquisition of this farm did not suit the political exigencies of the hon. Minister qf Marine
and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) and therefore the hon. Minister of Agriculture was compelled to buy the sand neap and pay $10,000 or $12,000 for something that is no good at all.
Hon. gentlemen may think I am speaking a little strongly about this but every -word I am saying is true. I am not painting it as black as it is. It is a pity, it is a shame, it is almost a crime that when New Brunswick, the one province in the whole of Canada that did not have an experimental farm, was to be provided with an experimental farm it should be given something which is worse than useless, squandering $27,000 or $28,000 in the initial stages and the Lord only knows what amount will be squandered by this Government in the future, notwithstanding the fact that they could .have found within the province thousands and tens of thousands of acres of as good land as can be found on the continent of America. My hon friend talks about finding fault with going to Fredericton; but I am not finding fault on that account.

I am not saying you
found fault.

Perhaps there is no place in the province of New Brunswick that is more accessible than the city of Fredericton, but if my hon. friend wanted to place this farm where it would be of the greatest use to the farming community he has gone to the wrong place, because Fredericton is not an agricultural community to any extent and it never will be a highly developed agricultural community.
