The Quebec Minister of Agriculture referred to the injury caused through the spread of tuberculosis among swine and cattle. In his opinion, the Dominion Government should apply part of the Dominion grant to the inspection of herds. I have carefully looked into the reports of the Quebec Minister of Agriculture, and I cannot find in it a single reference to the spread of tuberculosis. That disease was prevalent under the Liberal rule, and the hon. minister had not the courage to require the protection of his friends in Ottawa.
An easy answer to the Quebec Minister cf Agriculture is that the matter of cattle inspection cannot properly be included in an enactment concerning agricultural instruction. With a revenue of $13,000,000, the Quebec Government might surely protect our cattle against injury from tuberculosis.
But if Quebec has not the courage to grapple with the difficulty, if Quebec has not the courage to take the requisite means towards preventing the spread of bovine tuberculosis, I shall entreat the Dominion Government to undertake that work in the interest of the farmers of my province.
I protest most strenuously against the treatment dealt out to the farming class m the distribution of the Dominion grant; I am referring just now to the Minister of Agriculture for the province of Quebec. The following facts will surprise the farmers of our province and show to what use are put the moneys voted for agriculture.
In giving out the following information, I deem it preferable to leave out the family names of the men referred to. Mr. A. of the village of St. Roch des Aulnaies, county of l'lslet, was paid a thousand dollars by the Quebec Department of Agriculture, as superintendent of fruit-growing stations. That $1,000 did not come out of the Dominion grant, but was provided out of the treasury of the province of Quebec. He also received $100 for his travelling expenses. That appears on page 389 of the Public Accounts of the province of Quebec.
An hon. MEMBER; Why not give out the names?

Personally I have no objection, as they are under my hand. The person I have just referred to is Mr. Auguste Dupuis, of St. Roch des Aulnaies. Mr. Luc J. A. Dupuis, his nephew, of the same village of des Aulnaies, was paid $260 for lectures on agriculture. He has besides an account of $291 for travelling expenses.
Now, let us take up the Dominion grant
which has been granted to the same prov-

inoe of Quebec and with the distributing of which the Quebec Minister of Agriculture has been entrusted. For the fiscal year of 1912-13, I find that the same Auguste Dupuis has benefited by the Dominion grant to the extent of $497.52, for fruit trees, grafting, &c. Mr. Luc Dupuis, residing in the same village of des Aulnaies was paid $479 for lectures and travelling expenses.
On January 14, 1914, Mr. Tellier, leader of the Quebec Opposition, enquired from his seat in the local House what use had been made of the grant of $44,607.22 paid to the province on account of the Dominion grant to agriculture. Among various amounts paid out of that subsidy, I notice $165.65 to Mr. Luc J. A. Dupuis, of the village of des Aulnaies, for salary and expenses as instructor in bee-keeping. Mr. Luc J. A. Dupuis drew $532.70 as inspector of apiaries; Mr. P. A. Dupuis, $312.90 as assistant inspector of apiaries. Mr. L. J. A. Dupuis, the same person mentioned above, received $254.40 for the inspection of sugar bushes. Mr. Auguste Dupuis of the same village of des Aulnaies received $2,400 for fruit trees. Mr. L. J. A. Dupuis was paid $124.30 for inspecting illustration orchards.
According to a report filed at Quebec during the last session, the instructor in beekeeping, the inspector of apiaries, the assistant inspector of apiaries, the inspector of sugar bushes, the inspector of illustration orchards were all selected in the same family, in the same village, and I might almost say in the same household.
Through this political favouritism, the Minister of Agriculture of the province of Quebec runs counter to the most noble efforts of the farmers for the development of agriculture. Politicians have launched out their demands: agriculture is waning fast.
Thanks to the far-seeing efforts of our farmers, thanks to the zeal of the Dominion Government and of several provincial governments, agriculture will progress rapidly and the depletion of the country districts will cease. We will be in a position to let both producers and, consumers come to their own.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a few words on the question of the tobacco industry, especially in the counties of Essex and Kent. There has been a good deal of complaint and dissatisfaction amongst the tobacco growers. It is only a few years ago that the Parliament of Canada so altered the excise regulations that a considerable impetus was given to the tobacco industry. An experimental farm was also established by the
former Government at Harrow in the county of Essex. At one time tobacco growing in these counties was exceedingly profitable, but at the present time, although the crop has been a good and abundant one, the difficulty apparently is in not being able to obtain markets. The hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell) will know whether or not there are similar reports from the other tobacco growing parts of the Dominion, in the province of Quebec and the province of British Columbia. The difficulty is that, although the industry has a very considerable protection, the consumers apparently are getting no benefit from this protection, and the growers are getting no benefit. The suggestion is that there is an understanding, or combination, among the manufacturers which is keeping the price down to a point which renders tobacco growing unprofitable. The matter was brought to the attention of the Committee on Agriculture last week by my hon. colleague from West Kent (Mr. McCoig), and I understand that the Government had Mr. Barnet, who has charge of the experimental farm at Harrow, attend the meeting. By this time I would have thought that the minister would have had his report. My object in bringing the matter to his attention now is to know whether anything has been or is being done by the Government with the view of affording relief to those engaged in this industry. Some years ago there was a similar situa

tion. It was suggested that there was a combination of tobacco manufacturers, and the former Government appointed a commission. His Honour Judge MacTavish was sent out, he thoroughly investigated the conditions, and the result was that there was a considerable improvement. I do not know whether the Government is able to do anything, but if it can I would strongly urge upon the minister that some step should be taken in order to endeavour to get at the truth of the matter and see where the trouble lies.

While I am not thoroughly versed in all the. facts, I,think the situation is pretty much as my hon. friend states it. We have been doing something in regard to the tobacco industry chiefly to help it at the productive end in connection with methods o.f growing, of curing and putting up the leaf. The difficulty that is facing the grower now is absolutely and strictly a commercial question such as might turn up in any line of business. For instance, it turns , up to some extent in the fruit

growing industry. It is the question of the relationship between the buyer and seller. The situation is aggravated by reason of the fact that there are so few buyers that they can practically exercise a monopoly, or at all events be in a position to dictate to the producer the price that he shall take. Whether we can step in there is a question that reqjires consideration. I discussed the matter a little with my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) the other day. I do not know whether it has got to the point that the Government can step in and deal with it as a regular combine. I instructed Mr. Barnet who has charge of this work in Essex, to go to the meeting on Saturday, take a note of everything that was said and report to the department. I have not received his report; if it is yet in. It may net be in, but when we have gone further into the matter, if we find that we can do anything to relieve the situation, we will be glad to do it and I will let my hon. friend know.

I do not rise for
the purpose of criticising very much the remarks made by the hon. member for L'Islet (Mr. Paquet). Agriculture is a subject that, in my humble opinion, should be approached without any partisan spirit. I am only sorry to realize that my hon. friend from L'Islet has found it advisable to discuss this most important subject from a political point of view. When we sum up his whole speech we find it to be an unreasonable attack upon the Minister of Agriculture of the province of Quebec, Mr. Caron. I have no brief to defend in this House the action or the administration of the Department of Agriculture in the province of Quebec, but I believe that it is putting the question very fairly to say that in our province there is only one opinion regarding the administration of Mr. Caron. It is above reproach, and it deserves the favourable commendation of the whole people regardless of party politics. 'I think that my hon. friend from L'Islet remembers some of the bitterness of the political fight that took place in the county of L'Islet and in which, I am sorry to say, Mr. Caron was defeated. However that is, I believe the attack is unwarranted. My hon. friend found it advisable also to criticise the amount that is being voted annually by the Government of Quebec in aid of agriculture. He stated that the amount was half a million dollars or thereabouts. That .may be so but in fixing the 
amount at $500,000, or thereabouts, my hon. friend overlooks the immense amount of money which is being devoted to highways in our province, which is an indirect but great help to the farming community. He overlooks the great steel bridge industry which is being carried on so successfully in the province of Quebec and so advantageously to the farmer.

Is it not the same in
every other province?

I believe that the province of Quebec spent more money on highways this last year than any province in the Dominion regardless of population, and *that its expenditure exceeded that of the province of Ontario.
My hon. friend in criticising the item under discussion also referred to the high cost of living, and strange to say and to believe, the hon. member for L'Islet (Mr. Paquet) thought that the former Government was responsible for the present high cost of living in Canada, and tne reason he assigned for it was that we brought into this country too many immigrants who were consumers instead of producers. The very opposite is the case. The large majority of the immigrants brought into this country by the late Government as well as by this Government are producers and farmers, and not consumers in cities.
My hon. friend has also spoken of experimental farms. He extolled the beneficent action of the Conservative Government in regard to experimental farms. He referred especially to that farm which is known as Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere; but for some reason unknown to me, perhaps better known to himself, he refrained from telling this House who was the creator of that experimental farm. He could as well have said that it was entirely due to the efforts of my hon. friend from Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) and to the late Government.
Another point upon which I would like to touch very slightly is the small amount of increase in population in rural Quebec.
I think that my hon. friend stated that the rural population of the province of Quebec had increased by only 39,000. My hon. friend added that this increase was entirely applicable to villages and not to farming communities proper. My hon. friend then would conclude that the population in the rural districts proper, that is outside of the villages, has decreased. Does he know of many farms that have been abandoned in rural Quebec? Does he not know rather

that new towns, or parishes as we call them, entirely composed of farmers, have been established by dozens in the districts of Quebec alone?
I took the facts from the census.

No, the facts according
to the census are that the rural population has increased by 39,000. My hon. friend says that those are not farmers, that they are village residents. I say that they are farmers, because, in my whole district I do not know of ten farms that have been abandoned by farmers. On the contrary, I know of numbers of new parishes in the district of Quebec alone, entirely composed of farmers.
I really rose for the purpose of asking a few questions of the hon. Minister of Agriculture. I would like to know whether he has received a petition from the farmers of the county of Beauce, which I have the honour to represent, asking for the establishment of a branch station in that county or in the district. This matter was brought to the attention of the hon. minister last year. He promised then that he would give his earnest attention to it. I am informed this year that a largely signed petition has been sent to him asking for the establishment of an experimental farm or demonstration station in the district of Beauce. The reason the farmers in that district ask for such an establishment is the fact that they are remote from any experimental station. The nearest to them is, I think Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere, which is a long way off and hard to reach, the railway communication not being direct and the public having to go to Levi3 to get on to the Intercolonial line, and thence to Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere. The other station is at Cap Rouge, in the county of my hon. friend the Postmaster General; and as my hon. friend knows, it is also not very easy of access. I see in the item which was under discussion this afternoon an increase of $110,000 for the' maintenance of central iarms and establishment and maintaining of additional branch stations. Does the hon. minister contemplate establishing in the near future a branch station somewhere in the district of Beauce? This district is composed of the counties of Dorchester and Beauce, and would also take in the county of Megantic, and perhaps a part of the counties of Lot-biniere and Compton. This is essentially an agricultural community, and I think that no money could be spent more wisely
than by establishing a branch farm in that district. I would suggest to the minister, and I am sure that I will have the support of the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Sevigny) in this instance, that this branch farm be established in the county of Beauce, in that fertile valley called the Chaudiere Valley, where a model farm would be very easily provided and would be very accessible to all the farmers of the surrounding district. I would be pleased it the minister would make a positive declaration that he is going to grant this much-needed branch station in the county of Beauce.

I represent the county
situated next to Beauce. My hon. friend (Mr. Beland) and I very seldom agree; but on this point I must say to the hon. minister it is in the public interest to establish a branch station in that district composed of the counties of Beauce, Dorchester, Rellechasse, Levis, notbini&re and Megantic. My hon. friend from Beauce told us a few minutes ago that the station at Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere was established because the member for that county succeeded, when his party was in power, in getting such a station. I am sorry to say that the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) had not the same success in obtaining an experimental farm for our district when his party was in power, though I think a station of that kind was more wanted in the district of Beauce than in the county of Kamouraska. I hope to hear an expression on this subject from the hon. Minister of Agriculture. I should much like to have such a station in our district, and it goes without saying that I want it in the finest county of this Dominion, the county of Dorchester, which I represent. It will be in the same district, and so it will be very easy for the people of Beauce to come to my county. They can come with their member, and they may rest assured that we shall always be delighted to give them a good reception.

Mr. Chairman, I was aware that the hon. member for Beauce is an expert at speaking the tongue of Shakespeare, and I congratulate him in this connection, but representing as he does a French-speaking constituency of the province of Quebec, and having to deal with the remarks made by the hon. member for L'Islet, he should not, to my mind, have shown such disdain of his mother tongue as to demur answering him

in the language spoken by the great majority of his electors.
After tlhe example set by the hon. member for L'lslet, I take pleasure in congratulating the Dominion Government on its happy thought of encouraging agriculture by all possible means. Thus the very first year we appropriated a million dollars for that purpose. The second year we appropriated another million which was distributed among the various provinces and put at the disposal of the provincial ministers of agriculture in every case. It was not possible to do more, or to show a better disposition, and the most satisfactory results were expected. However, in spite of that material assistance provided by the Dominion Government, I am sorry to find that the amount allotted to the province of Quebec has not *been used quite in accordance with the purpose assigned to it. Far from it, in cases unfortunately too numerous, the grant was used not only towards inducing Liberal voters to vote against us, but even to create positions for opponents whom even we had dismissed. We made our own friends angry and laid ourselves open to reproof on their part, while at the same time we utterly failed to attain the object we were aiming at, which was to spread a knowledge of agriculture without distinction of party affiliations. From the experience acquired during the two last years, I come to the conclusion that, as regards the province of Quebec, it would be preferable to discontinue granting this subsidy and to establish instead experimental farms, rather than put these moneys in the hands of untrustworthy and shameless politicians as are to be found in the narrow circle of those holding power in Quebec.
I have just listened to the speech of the hon. member for L'Islet and his statements are not of a nature to surprise us in the least, knowing as we do the class of men with whom we have to deal in Quebec and who have given such strong evidence of grafting propensities of late. Partisanship is rife, and with their minds imbued with narrow prejudices, office holders are unable to rise above what they conceive to be in the interest of their party.
It is deeply to be regretted that the public funds appropriated to certain purposes by the Conservative party in Ottawa, should be put to such vile and Shameful use by the Quebec Liberal Administration. I may be allowed to give an instance. The county of Rimouski, which I have the honour to represent, has a population of 55,000 souls. Out of the Dominion grant voted for that

province, and which exceeded $109,000, how much do you think the Quebec Government *set aside for the county of Rimouski? The paltry sum of $326.39. That is what the Liberals have done to promote agriculture in the county of Rimouski. So I say that these moneys have been wrongly used, have been applied in the most unfair way, and if the distribution of the moneys is to be continued on those lines, it will be necessary to change our form of grant.
After listening to the particulars given by the hon. member for L'Islet, I agree with him that a revolting spirit of partisanship was exhibited by the Quebec Minister of Agriculture in fixing that amount of grant for his former constituency. Indeed the personal friends of the Quebec Minister of Agriculture have pocketed a total of $2,805.72, and the population of the county of L'lslet is only 16,000, while Rimouski, with a population of 55,000 souls, got only $326.39.
Thus we have, to the great satisfaction of the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) a fine school of agriculture in the county of Kamouraska, a school which gives excellent results, while in the counties of Temiscouata, Rimouski, Matane, Bonaven-ture, Gaspe, we find that practically nothing has been done to encourage our farmers and educate them, although the n ed for such .is more strongly felt in that part of the country than in any other. The county of Rimouski is especially in need of encouragement, its geographical situation resulting in a more rigorous climate. Our farmers have to contend against protracted and severe winters, late spr ng and early autumn frosts-frosts even during the summer season. It happens that we are obliged to keep the stock indoors for seven months in the year and over, and so I say the Government should make in our behalf heavier sacrifices than in behalf of more favoured localities. We have an excellent class of farmers, of undaunted courage and who would rejoice at seeing the Government intent on assisting them more efficiently through the establishment of a school of agriculture, let us say in the valley of the Matapedia, where it would be of use to the whole Gaspe peninsula, as well as to Rimouski and Matane.
Therefore I sincerely trust that the hon. minister will earnestly consider this question to which I already referred last year, when the estimates were before the House. As I said a moment ago fihat part

of the country should be the object of especial care on the part of the Government. We can make fine farming districts of the counties of Bonaventure and Gaspe, whereas at the present time the only class of people to be found there are fishermen, well worthy of our esteem, no doubt, but whose condition might be improved. As for the Liberal partisans, whose dealings have been severely criticised by the hon. member for L'Islet,
I am not surprised at t'heir conduct. Indifferent as they have shown themselves to be while in power to the real progress of agriculture, they continue, while in opposition, to secretly and stealthily put obstacles in the way of this Government's efforts towards bettering the conditions under which agriculture is carried on in this country.
Accordingly, the Bills which we had passed providing for the improvement of highways and the purchase of branch railways have been rejected by the Senate. Being jealous of the popularity accruing to the Conservative party on account of its far-seeing management of public affairs, and fearing with reason the effect that such wise administration would have, the L b-eral party is seeking to defeat that purpose by petty trtokery. They are not the true friends of the people those who act only through motives of spite and revenge, and the people in time will know who are their true friends.

Will my 'hon. friend allow me to ask a question? He has just stated that the Senate has rejected a Bill providing -a grant of money for the improvement of highways. He is well aware that such is not the case.

He does not know
better.

Does the hon. member
contend that the Senate has rejected this Bill?

The Senate amended
it in such a way as to render it utterly unacceptable.
Why did not the Government accept these amendments? .

Because the intention
was to distribute the funds for party ends. Let ns rise above petty party considerations when the 'agricultural interests of the country are at stake. When we are called upon to assist the settler, the hardy settler Who undertakes -to clear away the forest, with his axe and courage as bis only weapons, let us cordially respond to his appeal,
without inquiring whether 'he is Conservative or Liberal. Whatever his party .affiliations, the tiller of the soil is the man who supplies Canada with the muscle and brawn, which our population cannot forego. He is the purveyor of the national wealth of Canada, though he gets his full share of the hard labour, of the long hours, of the worry attendant on the expectation of a crop, which may he abundant and which may be wretched, according to the whims of the season. I say it once more, I regret that the true friends of the farmer should be so few; instead of being so few and far between, it seems that every hon. gentleman in this House should vie with his neighbours in finding some means of helping out the settler, whereas some find in their desire to further the ends of their party a sufficient excuse to withhold assistance from the agricultural interests, whatever form it may take.
That encouragement to agriculture is not lacking merely in the province of Quebec, but also in that of New Brunswick. While listening to the mover of the Address, the hon. member for York (Mr. McLeod), I could not help sympathizing personally with him when he referred to the loss of two representatives which awaits his province when the next redistribution of seats is effected. However, I do not think the constitution of the -country should be altered on that account. If New Brunswick has not the number of people requisite to retain its present number of representatives, it is due entirely to two main reasons which are Wholly dependent on its government.
1st. Continuous and speedy emigration of its people towards the western country;
2nd. Want of encouragement to agriculture.
Mr. Chairman, may I ask whether the rules of this House allow the reading of one's speech, and, if so, whefi has the rule 'been changed? I call your attention to that point.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I had noticed that the
hon. gentleman was reading.

Holding interests in that province, I concerned myself in latter years with the flow of emigration from the county of Rimouski along the line of the Intercolonial, a movement which has given rise to -compact farming communities made up of settlers who were only too glad to take possession of l-ands deserted by their original owners.
I travelled through the greater part of that province and I found a deplorable -state

of things. There practically exists no encouragement to agriculture. Cheese and butter factories which have done so much for the betterment of agriculture in the province of Quebec are non-existent in New Brunswick, despite the mildness of its climate and the fertility of its soil. Instead of there being a cheese or a butter factory in every parish, there is barely half a dozen all told throughout the province. The county of Rimouski, which I have the honour to represent, forms the northern boundary of New Brunswick. As a result, the climate is much more severe, notwithstanding which there is not a parish in that county but has its butter or cheese factory. Its government has been lacking in enterprise and apparently has offered no inducement to farmers' sons who have deserted by the thousand their fine province and followed the flow of emigration towards the West, a most deplorable state of things. Lands are being sold at a sacrifice to-day in New Brunswick, at half their value, in several counties. While land values have increased considerably throughout Canada, in New Brunswick they have remained at the same point, <and~even in many cases have decreased.
May I inquire from the hon. gentleman what part of New Brunswick he travelled through, what counties or parishes he visited?

I travelled through
practically the whole of New Brunswick, excepting the fine county of Madawaska. However, I may say to my hon. friend that I expect to pay him a visit next year.

My hon. friend will
then have, I hope, a more favourable report to make than the one he is now making.

As regards the cost of living this Government cannot be 'held responsible for it; though the former Government may be blamed for part of it, for not having done' what it should have done to promote agriculture, and I am willing to endorse the statement made by the hon. member for Belleehase (Mr. Lavelle) when moving the Address in answer to the Speech from the Throne:
Such is my sincere belief, Mr. Speaker, and I am satisfied that this same policy would successfully, and once for all, solve the problem of the high cost of living which has been growing on us for the last decade, and which has its starting point in the fact that agricultural production has not kept pace with the increase or population in business and industrial centres.
I say that within the last ten years the progress of agriculture, as well as of the live stock industry, has not been on a par with the growth

of population. The last census contains interesting statistics in this connection. They go to show that the population of several countries in the older provinces, instead of growing has diminished, and that business and manufacturing towns and cities have grown in proportion. Buie of thumb and slipshod methods have had the upper hand over the suggestions of a reasoned and progressive husbandry, such as would have resulted from a practical and painstaking teaching of agriculture. Accordingly we have witnessed the exodus of farmers' sons towards the cities, and the consequent scarcity of that labour with which farming cannot dispense.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I think the Government will never be able to extend enough encouragement to agriculture, for it is the source of the national wealth of the people and the country.
Mr. A. DeWITT FOSTER: I do not rise to offer any extended remarks upon this item, but I wish to take this opportunity of congratulating the Minister of Agriculture upon the very excellent work which the experimental farm has accomplished in the county which I have the honour to represent. At the outset, let me say that credit for the establishment of that farm is due, not only to the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell), but also to the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher), who does ,not at present occupy a seat in this House, but who, previous to the incoming of this Government, very gracefully accepted the gift of a farm in the vicinity of Kentville, for which the local Legislature, I think, paid some $11,000. The exMinister of Agriculture proceeded to spend some money in the development of that farm, and a fair amount of progress had been made when this Government came into power. That work has been rapidly pushed forward, to the great benefit of the farming communities, not only in the county of Kings, but of the adjacent counties in the western part of Nova Scotia as well. In connection with the operation of that farm, I would bring to the attention of the minister the suggestion of appointing on that farm a plant pathologist. With this addition, together with the other measures the minister has undertaken, we shall have in our midst one of the best experimental farms in Canada
The purpose for which I rose was-not to deal with this particularly, but to say a word with regard to an assertion made just a few moments ago by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland).
I have always listened to that hon. gentleman with most marked attention, and I am bound to say that of all the offerings from the Opposition, on ordinary occasions his sentences commend themselves to my-

self with quite as much force as do the remarks of any hon. member on that *side of the House. When, however, he said that the majority of immigrants into Canada during the last ten, twelve or fifteen years, has consisted of farmers, farm labourers and producers, I think his statement is subject to some slight correction. I may not be able to give that correction in its fullest detail, but there are some figures which I have gathered which I think would be of advantage and interest to the members of the committee, and with the indulgence of the Chairman and hon. members I would like to place them on ' Hansard ' for future reference in connection, particularly, with the high cost of living. It has been argued, and, I think, justly so, that the high cost of living is due to the lack of producers in Canada; that is to say, the lack of farmers or men who till the soil and help to extract [DOT] wealth therefrom. It is a startling fact that since 1901, notwithstanding the organized efforts of both out-going and the present Government, the rural population in Canada has increased only 17.10 per cent, while the urban population has increased 62.25 per cent. The total immigration of Canada has grown from 21,176 in 1897 to 402,432 in 1912-13. In 1897 we had
11,000	immigrants of British origin, 2,000 from the United States, and 8,000 from all other places. In 1912-13, the British-born aggregated 151,000, the newcomers from the United- States 139,000, while from other sources we drew 113,000, making in all over
400,000.	There is no gainsaying the fact that in 1900 the tide of immigration began somewhat with a rush, not, we might say, with the best class of immigrants, but a very large portion of them were desirable for the uplifting of this great Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I call your attention to the fact that the honoui-able member is out of order, when discussing immigration in connection with this item.

The hon. member for Montcalm is asking whether or not the hon. member is out of order in the remarks which he is now making. It should be sufficient to state that the item under discussion is the administration and enforcement of the Destructive Insect and Pest Act. I may say for the information of the hon. member for Montcalm that there was an understanding at the last sitting of the comimttee that hon. members would be allowed to go on, under the two preceding
items, Patent Record and Experimental Farms. So long as the hon. gentleman keeps to these two items and the one at present under discussion, he is in order.

In bringing this
matter to your attention, Mr. Chairman, I was under the impression that I was speaking under the item of Experimental Farms, and inasmuch as all experimental farm work has to do with the increase of production from the soil, it did seem to me that my remarks were somewhat pertinent.
Go on.

In ten years, from 1903
to 1913, a total of 973,730 English immigrants came into the Dominion of Canada: these include, of course, Welsh, Scotch and Irish immigrants. From the United States we had 891,129, and from other sources 656,255. Of the latter number, there were of Austro-Hungarians,	164,527;	Chinese, 25,016;
French, 21,085; Austro-Germans, 30,762; Hebrews, 61,384; Italians, 88,008; Japanese, 14,617; Polish, 24,396; Russians, 67,378; Finnish, 17,535; Swedish, 24,220; Norwegians, 17,322; and smaller numbers of Belgians, Bulgarians, Greeks, Roumanians, Swiss, Danes, Icelanders, Turks, Syrians, Hindus. The total immigration in this period was 2,521,144. But here is the interesting uoint. In the last ten years there came to this country 866,916 farmers, including farm labourers, which, you will see, is less than one-third of the total amount of immigration that has come to this country during that period. There were 898,916 general labourers, mechanics, etc., and, in addition to that, 174,896 clerks, traders and miners. The greater part of the increase in Canada has been crowding into the urban centres, as was shown by the first statement I made, that rural population has increased a little over 17 per cent while the urban population has increased over 62 per cent, -so that the greater part of these must have gone to the cities. The fact is made more clear when we remember that ten years ago, in 1901, the cities in this Dominion had a population of some two millions, and they have been receiving an average immigrant influx of nearly 165,000 per annum, or 1,650,000 in 10 years. These are the people whom we have had to employ in Canada, have had to house and feed and find places for, in the cities largely, and it is this class of people who, while eventually we will be able to assimilate them, constitute to-day

one of the great factors in causing the high cost of living in Canada. We must remember that when the United States had 70,000,000 people, their immigration was only
400,000	per year, and the records will ishow that they were hardly able to assimilate them at that rate. We in Canada, with only eight million people, are endeavouring to do what the United States people did with seventy millions or more, namely, assimilate 400,000 people a year of various nationalities. I might go on and give you a comparative statement of the rural and urban population, but, in order not to take up time on this particular item, I shall reserve that until some future occasion.

I desire to say a word or two, not by way of criticism particularly of the minister, but to call his attention to a matter which I think it is my duty to do, owing to what appears to be a great disparity in the expenditure of moneys under this heading. At page 17 of the Agricultural Gazette, which has run the gauntlet of a very fierce fire from hon. gentlemen opposite, they will notice that the number of branch farms and stations is set out by name and place. I have taken the trouble to tabulate them and I find that under this heading there are in the province of Quebec 1,051 acres established for experimental purposes; in British Columbia, 1,578 acres; in Nova Beotia 594 acres; in New Brunswick, 450 acres; in Manitoba, 680 acres; in Saskatchewan, 1,032 acres; in Alberta, 890 acres; in Prince Edward Island, 100 acres and in the province of Ontario just 40 acres. Coming from that province, and although I am not entrusted with any brief on behalf of the province of Ontario, I could not help but feel, as a representative of one of the counties there, that this is a matter which should be brought to	the	attention
specifically of the hon. Minister of Agriculture, coupled with a request that where there is	such a great
disparity and inasmuch as the forty acres that are set apart for that cause in the province of Ontario are entirely devoted to experimentation on tobacco plants, the great basic industries of the province are entirely neglected; while, for example, in the province of Quebec, which has been the subject of great complaint against the minister to-night, I find there are established farms at Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere, 235 acres; at Cap Eouge, 326 acres; at Farnham, 60 acres; and just recently purchased at Lennoxville, Quebec, 430 acres for a new

experimental farm; making for
10 p.m. the province of Quebec 1,051 acres; while there are 40 acres for tobacco only, in the province'of Ontario. The point I wish to make is that you cannot satisfy our friends from Quebec tonight. They have made a most aggravated attack upon the hon. Minister of Agriculture because this particular farm was not right or that farm was not right, and the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., complained that the school was in the wrong place, that the farm was sixty-five miles away from it, that everything was going to the bowwows. I want the hon. minister to cut out these men who are complaining, and go up to the province of Ontario and give us an expenditure of a few hundred thousand dollars in the newer part of the province to establish farms upon the soils that have yet to be cultivated, treated and understood. He will find there a receptive people who will be thankful to him for the benefits he will give to that province and I know he will never be met with such complaining, carping criticism as has been revealed from these gentlemen on the other side of the House for whom he has done so much.

Would the minister give an
outline of the work- that is being done at Farnham, and also state what the land cost?

I do not think I can
give all the details the non. gentleman wants and if he does not mind I shall leave this until my Estimates are again under consideration when I can make a complete statement.
I might say a word in reply to the various gentlemen who have spoken on the experimental farms' vote which has already passed the committee. I could not quite follow some of the criticisms, not alone from our friends in French, which I cannot follow very well, unfortunately, but I could not follow very well the line of criticism followed by some hon. gentlemen opposite, especially the hon. member for North Oxford. 1 gather that his general line of complaint in connection with the whole experimental farm question was that the revenue derived from it was exceedingly small and the expense intolerably large. I would point out to him that no man who has ever given this matter any study at all would expect an experimental farm to pay. It is obvious that if you are going to carry out thirty, forty, or a hundred lines of research of experimental work, perhaps 99 per cent

of which must be discarded after long study, it is impossible to make it pay in a commercial sense. I was also surprised because, although he seemed to deprecate the idea of scientific work, he gave certain testimony to-day by approving of such work as that which is done under the cow-testing record branch which requires scientific training, a knowledge of Babcock testing, a knowledge of systems of feeding and methods of finding out what amount of butter fat there is in milk, all of which is of a scientific character and which we are concerned with in our experimental work both on the farms and elsewhere. A good many gentlemen have spoken of the need of these farms in various portions of the country. The hon. member for Beauce has asked me if I have received a petition from his county. I have, and I wish to inform him that it is one, I think, of forty or fifty. I might almost say one hundred counties from which I have received similar petitions and which probably my predecessor as Minister of Agriculture had also received before me. It is true that we have not gone as fast as some of our friends in the country would wish, but at the present time we are spending approximately on the general experimental farm system three times the amount spent only two years ago. We are therefore making some headway. There is this distinction between what I may call experimental farm work and the class of work to which I think most of the gentlemen have alluded to-night. It is eminently fitting that the federal Government should deal with experimental and research work of a national character, but I have always felt that purely demonstration work is a matter more for provinces and local authorities. I admit that the field is a very big one, that there is need for all activities federal and provincial. I am not in a position to make any definite promises as to any particular section, but I think, myself, that there will have to be some broadening out and expanding so that if the provinces do not take a more forward step we shall have to invade that field as well. Some provinces like my own are already carrying out demonstration work under our Agricultural Instruction Act, but if the provinces do not move fast enough I am not at all sure that we shall not meet tnat condition-we shall think it over most carefully-by tying up small stations of the demonstration type to our experimental farm system. I shall probably be able to make some move in that direction before long. I would not, however, like to make any promise in regard to any special districts to-day nor would I like to adjudicate as between Beauce and Dorchester. It may be true as my hon. friend said that his farm was coming veTy rapidly in 1911. It is a great thing to entertain large and generous hopes.
I think I can now give the hon. member for Edmonton a little more definite information in Tegard to what we are doing against the devastating ravages of the cutworm and the eelworm in southern Alberta. That cutworm destroyed 30,000 to 40,000 acres of wheat in Alberta in 1912. Mr. Strickland, an entomologist whom we had already taken into our employ a little before for that kind of work, has been making a study of it and has done some good work. We cannot say what practical results will be achieved because this is a new species and differentiated from the ordinary cutworm in that it does not feed above ground, consequently the usual methods of control 3uch as poisoned bran, and so on are no good in this case. Mr. Strickland has been making a study of the life history of the insect with a view to devising some control. It is gratifying to know that the insect was far less destructive last year and I think the chances are that next year and following years we may not have the same trouble at all; but we shall continue to make a study of the life history of the insect and the b3st methods of controlling it. We cannot say anything very definite in regard to the eelworm which is not an insect proper but a white microscopic worm, sometimes parasitic and sometimes feeding on vegetation, and in some parts of Europe on cereals. We have not yet arrived at any conclusion in regard to this infestation. We have not even been able to decide whether it was the cause of the killing of the winter wheat. The wneat may have been killed partly through the soil, and partly through climatic conditions. Mr. Strickland will go on studying that matter. We are also in correspondence with men in various parts of the world who have given special attention to that class of pest and any work we can do along that line will be prosecuted in the interests of the country.

Has it been possible to
secure information as to similar pests elsewhere in the world?

We are endeavouring to get that now. There is not a very full supply of information on this particular class

of organism, but some work has been done in Europe and in the United States where Ur. Howard is only too willing to help us.

The main point is that
the department recognize that there is a serious condition and is using every possible means to combat it.
Undoubtedly.

Mr. [DOT]Chairman, the hon. member for L'Islet has severely criticised the conduct of the Quebec Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Caron) in connection with the distribution of public moneys voted by the Dominion Government for the benefit of the province of Quebec. The hon. gentleman referred to what I said when moving the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, and made me state that the Dominion Government had not done anything for the farmers. That is not what I said. I stated that there was nothing in the Speech from the Throne showing that the Government intended to extend assistance to the farming class. The hon. gentleman stated that the Quebec Government had wasted, spent right and left, the moneys appropriated by the Dominion Government for the promotion of agriculture; that the Quebec authorities had shown themselves to be poor managers. To that I shall oniy answer: What was the verdict of the farming class themselves in the general provincial elections held on May 15th, 1912? Every Conservative candidate was utterly defeated, after preaching that doctrine of bad management on the part of the Minister of Agriculture of the Province of Quebec. The hon. Mr. Caron is a practical man, an agriculturist of note, and the success he has won since he has entered the Quebec cabinet is evidence of the truth of my contention.
The member for L'Islet has no reason to thus run him down. I would like to see the member for L'Islet filling the position held by Mr. Caron; I wonder if he would work wonders as compared with Mr. Caron. It is an easy matter to find fault, to condemn, to criticise all that is being done, but it is quite another story when it comes to improving on present conditions.
The member for L'Islet would have as believe that the friends of the farming class are the Conservatives. He has stated over and over again that the policy of the Conservative party, since its coming into power at Ottawa, had been worthy of admiration, that the Department of Agriculture had accomplished great things. I am in a measure interested in agricultural pursuits, and I wonder if the member for L'Islet is aware
fMr. Burrell. 1
of what I am going to state. Is he aware that out of the Dominion grant towards promoting agriculture in the various provinces, it was at first understood with the provincial ministers of agriculture that a certain amount would be applied to the drainage cf farm lands?

Will the hon. member
allow me to reply? I stated that the Act of 1912 provided for improvements in general.

I wish the hon. gentleman would wait till I am through. He is not here to run the House. Though his friends are in power, we have the right to speak as well as he has himself. So I was saying that the Dominion Minister of Agriculture had authorized the Quebec Minister of Agriculture to apply part of those moneys to furthering' the drainage of farm lands. That held good until lately. But those good friends of the farmers, those natural protectors of the farming class, have just repealed that clause of the Act. They are no longer willing to further the drainage of our lands. That is what I had to say to the member for L'Islet, who boasts of the extraordinary measure of protection farmers receive at the hands of the Department oi Agriculture, when it has just repealed a provision which was of great benefit to them. If the Conservative Government is the friend of the farming class, why do they not take some means of protecting them? Their friendship is as short-lived as the bloom of roses.
Why does not the Government do away with the duty on agricultural implements? Possibly your reply will be that neither has my party done so. I was right in stating that there is nothing in the Speech from the Throne to protect the farmers. Do away with the duty on agricultural implements, and then you may boast of having done something helpful to the farming community. Why not do away with the duties on chemical fertilizers, on German fertilizers, for instance, which are taxed at the rate of $50 a ton? That is what you should do, you who say you are the friends of the farmers. Country folks are not very fond of such friends.
You the friends of the people? Why then not do away with the cattle embargo? Your ministers are taking pleasure trips in every direction at the expense of the State. What steps have they taken towards doing away with the Canadian cattle embargo? There is not a cent voted for the suppression cf that embargo, of that hideous embargo, and you say you are the friends of the farmer! If you are really the friends of the farmer,

why do you not cut down the duties on agricultural implements and on commercial fertilizers, and why do you not do away with the cattle embargo? No you are only mock friends, and I have no use for that kind.
Besides, Canadian tobacco is not sufficiently protected. The duty should be raised live cents a pound. The Government is doing absolutely nothing to further tobaccogrowing. Under the former Government, the duty was raised to 28 cents per pound, in order to protect Canadian tobacco against competition from the foreign leaf, and it was owing to that enactment that tobaccogrowing has been made a success in various counties, such as Montcalm and Essex. It was not through the efforts of the Conservatives that tobacco-growing developed. I deny that. It developed through the efforts of the Liberals. But the measure of protection granted at the time is no longer adequate. The duty should be raised five cents per pound in order to protect our home grown leaf against the competition of the United States leaf. Petition after petition is forwarded, appeal after appeal is being made to you, resolution after resolution is being passed by business men requesting the government to endeavour to make a success of Canada's world-fair. And the Government makes no move.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon.
gentleman has no right to discuss an item previously voted. He should confine himself to experimental stations and patents.
When hon. gentlemen on this side of the House have the floor, there is no occasion, Mr. Chairman, for drawing your attention to irregularities.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It was understood that illustration stations and patents would today be the subject-matter of discussion, b it not items previously considered. I hope the hon. gentleman will confine his remarks to the item under consideration. I do not wish to interrupt him, but only to draw his attention to the matter.

You do not wish to interrupt me, but you cut me short all the same. That is an odd way of dealing with people. On several occasions, Mr. Chairman, the establishment of agricultural stations throughout the Dominion has been urged, by myself amongst others. I said the Speech from the Throne contained no reference showing that the Government intends to establish any such stations. The experimental farm at Ottawa is a necessity, I agree; but, on the other hand, it is neces-74
sary that there should be a dismemberment of that farm and that stations be estahlishe 1 in various parts of the country. Does tbe Government state that its intention is to comply in the near future with the wishes of the farming community? Hon. gentlemen are deaf. They speak not.
Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ask a question? Is he in favour of establishing an experimental farm in the county of Dorchester?
I want some every where, but let them start one first in Mont calm.
Is the hon. gentleman anxious for one in Dorchester county?
If the hon. gentleman from Nicolet wishes to speak, let him wait until I am through.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman objects to being interrupted, he should be allowed to go on.

I am anxious to have experiment stations established in all large centres, be it Dorchester, Nicolet, Montcalm or any other place. Whatever pertains io agriculture is of interest to me, and I am ready to fight for it. It is a matter of fair play, with which party politics have nothing to do. Besides, I shall have occasion to make further reference to the subject later on.
As I stated previously, the experimental farm at Ottawa has surely its usefulness, and whatever amount is spent through it, I shall not complain. But farmers will reap greater benefit from agricultural stations situated in their vicinity. I wish to draw the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to the fact that those district experiment stations should be put in a position to distribute larger quantities of seed grain. That should be one of the services rendered by such stations. I regret to find that the farmers of the Province of Quebec do not apply to the Central Experimental Farm at Ottawa for larger quantities of that seed grain. The farmers of the Province of Ontario are away ahead of us in that respect. The Government representing itself as the friend, the protector of the farming class, should be in a position to accomplish a little more than formerly. Well, through the establishment of those experiment stations and the distribution of such seed grain, by their means actual headway will be made.
I thank you, Mr. Chairman, for having allowed me to make these few remarks. 1

shall have occasion to revert later on to that subject of agriculture, in connection with some other item. I wished to state and I do state that it is not the Conservative party, but the Liberal party that is the true friend of the farmer. It was the Liberals who protected the farmers more than they had ever been protected in the past.

Mr. Chairman, I think it incumbent upon me, in spite of the lateness of the hour, to ask permission to say a few words on a subject of such great importance as that just now being considered by this Committee. Agriculture, in general, is unquestionably the most important matter that can be taken up by a body of men such as those congregated in this House. It is assuredly the only one of the various industries of interest to the public in which one may rest assured that the capital invested will never be lost. But, in order to succeed therein there is need for extensive knowledge, a good deal of brain work, and governments the world over make it a point to further its continued progress by all means possible.
I sincerely believe that the former Minister of Agriculture has done for the farming class as much as it was possible to do with the funds at his disposal. But I must admit, that this Government has taken a position unprecedented in the history of Canada as regards the furthering of agricultural pursuits. The current appropriations have been greatly increased, and besides, a special vote has been taken providing a million dollars per annum towards agricultural instruction in general. A new impetus has been given to the work of the cow-testing associations and to the improvement of all kinds of live stock, through the greater facilities afforded in the use of the proper foundation stock. I am glad to be able to congratulate the hon. Mr. Burrell, who is at the head of the department of Agriculture, on the good work he has been doing since he holds the portfolio, and on the satisfactory results he has obtained.
In passing, I may state that my hon. friend the member for Montcalm (Mr. La-fortune) was contending a moment ago that under the Act for agricultural instruction, the experiments in drainage started last year had been discontinued through the unwillingness of the Minister. I have in my hand a public document setting forth the objects for which the $159,000 placed for the current year at the disposal of the Province of Quebec had been expended and I find the following: illustrations m draining, $12,000.

year the grant to the Province of Quebec amounted to $139,000, and this year it amounts to $159,000, and it is in the statement showing the distribution of that $139,000 that I find $12,000 for drainage.
Reference has been made to-night to experiment stations. I may be allowed to say that owing to the startling variations in climate to be observed in passing from one district to the other, that policy of having numerous experiment stations, can never be furthered too actively and energetically, especially in its eastern and northern parts. The eastern part of the Province of Quebec, not to say the whole province, has within the last seven years suffered through a succession of bad crops, of a nature to discourage the most determined. The complaint in certain parts is that the population in the country districts is on the decline and is emigrating to the cities. It is no wonder that, following on a succession of reverses, so trying and vexatious as those I have referred to, some should lose heart and should endeavour to find some other means of securing those comforts of life, which after all are necessary in a measure, and with that in view should resort to emigration. It is mueh to be regretted that in such an age as this, when people seem to have lost their heads and to think that comfort, and even luxury, are the main objects of life, our farming class should *have met with a succession of poor crops. Such an unfortunate concourse of circumstances have necessarily had a depressing effect and resulted in the depletion of the country population, a fact which all deplore.
It is much to be regretted that the Quebec Government, about which there is so much talk, should not have deemed proper, being more particularly entrusted with the welfare of the inhabitants of that province, to get right down to work and try to discover the means of safeguarding the farming community under its care against those changes of temperature or other scourges which Providence has in store, in such a way that they would be left, even under adverse conditions, with a modicum of a crop.
Formerly, in some of the far nothern districts of the Northwest, it was found absolutely impossible to produce grain of good quality in fair quantities. Governments have taken up the question; farmers, meeting with a series of uninterrupted failures, set themselves to working out the problem, and to-day in those localities where it was

not possible to find five per cent of good grain in the year's crop, turn out millions of bushels of No. 1 grain every year.
If study, intelligence and industry have in the West given such marvellous results, I wonder if the same means would not, when taken in the Province of Quebec, produce exactly the same results. The idea did not even occur to the Government of the Province of Quebec that something might be done towards finding a remedy to the ills of agriculture under such circumstances.
An interest has been developed in good roads, which is a very good thing, but good roads lose a good deal of their usefulness when there is no traffic to circulate over them. I say therefore that the Quebec Government have completely erred, shown a lack of enterprise and earnestness, inasmuch as they have caused the farming class to turn their attention to other matters of some interest to them, no doubt, but at the same time caused them to neglect other matters of still greater moment. What will he the use of good roads, if the farmers have no produce to draw over them? To my mind, it would be better for them to have abundant crops as they have in the West, though traffic may be blocked for want of means of transportation, rather than have highways or transportation facilities and no produce for home consumption. That is what has happened in the Province of Quebec during the last decade. So I think it behoove3 me to draw the attention of the Dominion Government and of this House to the ridiculous position in which the district of Quebec, if not the Province of Quebec, is being put, and to induce, if possible, the Minister of Agriculture, when negotiating the next agreement with the Quebec Government, to require the Quebec Minister of Agriculture to take up first and carry on such experiments as I have pointed out.
At a not very remote period, the Province of Quebec could boast of leading the Dominion in the matter of dairying. It was recognized that out of ten cheese or butter factories, nine were good, and only one, inferior. Gn the third of December last, at the convention of the Dairymen's Association of the Province of Quebec, the representative of the Montreal cheese trade, addressing a large audience, comprising, if my memory is good, the provincial Minister of Agriculture and his deputy minister, stated that he was sorry to have to warn the Province of Quebec that at present, out of ten cheese or butter factories in that province, there were nine bad, and only one good. That was rather startling information, of a nature to grate on the feelings of 74J
the people of that province, and more particularly of its government and Minister cf Agriculture, who proclaim so loudly their devotion to the imblie weal.
Farmers generally take an interest in crop-growing, as well as in milk production. Those two items make up 95 per cent of the revenue of the farming class in Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, that being well understood,, what shall we say of the policy of the Government which, after witnessing the drift of things, flatter themselves with finding a. remedy in a good roads policy, even though it entails the mortgaging of municipalities for a period of 41 years, with almost ruinous-consequences to some of them, and then prevents the Dominion Government fronv granting to its province hundreds of thousand dollars, part of which might surely have been applied to partly paying off every year the aforesaid mortgage. Hon. gentlemen will admit, no doubt, that representing as 1 do an agricultural constituency, it is incumbent on me to draw the attention of this House and of the Minister of Agriculture to the way matters are being managed in the Province of Quebec, and to request the men holding power in Ottawa to firmly take in hand the interests of my province and of my county, so that the Dominion subsidy granted by us may be put to a more practical use than heretofore.
I may be allowed to state that the agreement entered into by the Quebec and the Ottawa ministers in the last two years, h is given results far from satisfactory to those members of the Quebec district who support this Government. We are supposed to know the requirements of the province and of oar various counties as well as, if not better than, one or two government men in Quebec who utterly fail to take a broad view of the requirements of agriculture, and for the last ten years have allowed the farming class in Quebec to lose ground in the woeful way I have pointed out; and I am satisfied that the time has come when, perforce, the Government providing the funds to assist the farmers of my province must take upon itself, acting on the information supplied by us, to lay down its terms and see to it that the general interest be safeguarded in preference to those of individuals, the latter having had the upper hand during these last two years, under the arrangements as taken.
Of course, in view of the facts just referred to, experimental research work will be in order in the eastern and northern parts of my province, so as to render as expeditiously as possible' agriculture a paying and attractive venture. Unless that is done the depletion of population which is complained

of, will be growing worse, and the ills whi :h all deplore will continue developing from day to day.
Many references have been made to experiment stations to-night. Every hon. member wants one for his own constituency, though not objecting to others being treated alike. Let me say that the Dominion Government having at present in the Province of Quebec experimental farms organized or about to be organized in the Eastern Townships, where the climate is mild, in the vicinity of Quebec, for the middle region, and at Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere, for the South shore, that number, considering the transportation facilities which are now everywhere at hand, should afford a fair measure of service to the major part of the province, until the time comes when the Government will be in a position to provide one farm per county, if required, which, I think, would be a very good idea.
But I have the honour to represent here a district which from the geographical viewpoint occupies a very peculiar position. Its climate is different from that of Quebec, it rests on a geological formation different from that at Quebec; there Spring is always later than elsewhere; even the forest growth has a different appearance from that to the south of the Laurentian range. There is to be found there a population of about 40,000 souls which is making a pretty good living, thank God, but under climatic and other conditions to be found no where else in the Province of Quebec. The fight which the farmers have to put up in that district against adverse conditions of every description-even when Providence extends its beneficent hand here as elsewhere-is necessarily much more strenuous. So I say it behooves the various governments with which my constituents have to do, to confer on them that great boon that they have been in need of for sixty years past and that they have been applying for through petitions, delegations and all possible means from the Dominion Government, for the last ten years.
" I appeal to the good faith of all my colleagues from the Province of Quebec: this [DOT] is no question of party politics, it is a simple question of business, common sense and equity. I contend that with the experimental farms at present in existence in the Province of Quebec, the general interests are thoroughly looked after for the time being, and if the Government be disposed, as I understand it, is to grant to them experimental farms, the district where that policy should be carried out in the first place is that ot

Chicoutimi and Lake St. John, which I have the honour to represent,
Before I resume my seat, Mr. Chairman, I wish to draw the attention of the Minister to the importance for him, if he wishes to actually be of assistance to the Province of Quebec, of making arrangements for carrying on in the course of this year, on the farms at Cap Rouge, and more particularly at Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere, experiments in the growing of winter grain, which has been the salvation of the West and shou'd be the salvation also of the Province of Quebec. I understand that one of his head officers has been carrying on such expen-ments on his own farm in the district of Quebec. I know that a few fanners have carried on such experiments at home, with invariably satisfactory results. So I say it is urgent that the Minister should himself carry on such experiments, in order to be in a position to lay official data before the public. It is practically a question of life and death for the farming class of Quebec that they be assured every year of fair returns from their seeding, as are secured in the West. I thank you, Mr. Chairman, for your kindness in allowing me to make these few remarks.
